The cliff everyone can see coming
Meanwhile, Western pharma is staring at a number that keeps its CFOs awake.
Over
$230 billion
in biopharma revenue loses patent exclusivity by 2030. For some mega-cap companies, that's up to
65% of current sales
exposed to generic and biosimilar competition.
The centerpiece is
Keytruda
. Merck's checkpoint inhibitor generates tens of billions annually, anchors the company's valuation, and goes off patent in the U.S. in
late 2028
. There is no organic pipeline on Earth that replaces that revenue on that timeline. The only lever is acquisition.
So M&A came back, violently. After a sluggish stretch of high interest rates, aggregate deal value rebounded to somewhere between
$133 billion and $240 billion
globally across 2025 and early 2026.
The character of the deals is telling. Nobody is buying diversification. Acquirers want de-risked, clinical-stage assets in three areas — oncology, cardiovascular-renal-metabolic, immunology — and they want them now:
Vertex
paid
$10 billion
for Crinetics Pharmaceuticals, largely for paltusotine in rare hormone disorders
Merck KGaA
paid
$11.3 billion
for Bio-Techne, a life-sciences toolmaker — buying picks and shovels, not gold
GSK
paid
$10.6 billion
for Nuvalent to reinforce its lung cancer pipeline
And a new instinct has emerged that Bain calls
"buy the factory, not just the drug."
In radiopharmaceuticals — where the medicine is radioactive, decays on a clock, and must reach a patient within hours — over
80% of 2025 deals
explicitly included manufacturing or isotope supply chain integration. Owning a brilliant molecule means nothing if you can't get sterile fill-finish capacity. Post-BIOSECURE, that lesson has generalized.
The startup ecosystem feeding this machine remains stubbornly concentrated in the San Francisco Bay Area.
Parvus Therapeutics
in Burlingame is developing in vivo regulatory T cell therapies for autoimmune disease using pMHC nanomedicines — teaching the immune system to stand down rather than suppressing it wholesale, partnered with AbbVie. Genesis Therapeutics sits in the same neighborhood. Both are the kind of
platform
company big pharma now prefers to acquire: not one drug, but a machine that makes drugs.
To bridge the gap between founders who believe their platform is worth a fortune and buyers who've been burned before, deals increasingly use
Contingent Value Rights
— payouts tied to specific clinical milestones. Half the money now, the other half if the thing actually works.
Part VI: The Twenty-Year Horizon
Everything so far is the present tense. Here's where it goes.
The next phase of pharmaceutical ambition moves from
localized
problems — a specific mutation in a specific tumor — to
systemic
ones: the diffuse, multi-causal failures of human biology that have humbled every approach thrown at them.
Alzheimer's: the end of the single-target era
For thirty years, Alzheimer's research was organized around one hypothesis. Amyloid-beta plaques accumulate in the brain; clear the plaques, stop the disease. The field pursued it with a focus that critics called monomaniacal and defenders called rigorous, and it produced one of the worst failure records in the history of clinical medicine.
Amyloid-clearing antibodies —
lecanemab
(Leqembi) and
donanemab
(Kisunla) — finally worked, in the narrow sense that they modify disease progression. They are not cures, and the reason cuts to the heart of the problem: by the time a patient walks into a clinic with symptomatic dementia, amyloid has been accumulating for
fifteen to twenty years
. The neural damage is done. You've arrived at the fire with a hose, twenty years after the building burned.
The pipeline for the 2030s reflects a much more honest reading of the biology. In 2026, nearly
200 clinical trials
are assessing over
150 candidate therapies
, most of them aimed at mechanisms other than amyloid:
Chronic neuroinflammation
— microglia, the brain's resident immune cells, shifting from housekeepers to arsonists
Metabolic resilience
— mitochondrial bioenergetics, because neurons are enormously expensive cells to run and an aging brain runs a power deficit
Vascular health
— the increasingly clear overlap between cardiovascular disease and dementia
Tau pathology
— the tangles inside neurons, which track cognitive decline considerably better than plaques ever did
There's even a serious effort to repurpose
GLP-1 analogues
— the diabetes and obesity drugs — for their downstream neuroprotective and metabolic effects in the brain. Ozempic for Alzheimer's sounds like a bad headline. It's a real hypothesis with real mechanistic grounding.
The endgame looks like modern oncology. Not one magic bullet, but AI-driven multi-omics defining biological subtypes of Alzheimer's, each getting a precision combination therapy — the same way "breast cancer" fractured into a dozen molecularly distinct diseases with a dozen different treatment algorithms.
Diagnostics are moving in lockstep, and this may matter more than any drug. Blood biomarkers — particularly phosphorylated tau
p-tau217
and alpha-synuclein — can detect Alzheimer's and Lewy body pathology
years before cognitive symptoms appear
. A blood test, not a PET scan or a spinal tap. That changes the treatable window from "after the damage" to "before it."
And on the delivery side,
focused ultrasound
can temporarily open the blood-brain barrier — the physiological fortress that has blocked the majority of CNS drug candidates for a century — letting large biologics into neural tissue on demand.
Put those together and the plausible endpoint is this: Alzheimer's becomes a chronic managed condition. Detected early by blood test, subtyped by multi-omics, treated with combination therapy delivered past the barrier. Not cured. Managed. For a disease that currently kills everyone it touches, managed would be a revolution.
Fluorescence micrograph of cultured brain cells with neurons labeled in green and red
Cultured brain cells, labeled by antibody staining. By the time dementia symptoms appear, amyloid has been accumulating in tissue like this for two decades. The next generation of drugs aims at the window before that. (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA)
Longevity: the honest version
Now for the promise that generates the most breathless coverage and deserves the most skepticism.
Prominent voices in tech have suggested AI could effectively "cure" aging and double human lifespan by
2033
.
The demographic evidence says no. An analysis published in
Nature Aging
concluded that radical life extension is implausible this century absent a fundamental, systemic slowing of biological aging. The reason is arithmetic rather than pessimism: in developed countries, we have already harvested nearly all the gains available from reducing early- and mid-life mortality. Sanitation, antibiotics, vaccines, cardiac care, seatbelts — the easy decades are spent. What's left is the biology of aging itself, and we have not moved it.
The
TAME trial
— Targeting Aging with Metformin — is the cautionary tale. It proposes to test a cheap generic drug against a composite endpoint of cardiovascular disease, cancer, dementia, and all-cause mortality. It is elegant, important, and has been stalled for a decade, because metformin is off-patent and nobody can monetize the answer. The market does not fund questions it cannot own.
But here is the distinction that gets flattened in the coverage:
lifespan and healthspan are not the same variable.
Healthspan — years lived free of chronic, debilitating disease — is poised for genuine expansion by 2045, and the investment is flowing toward three mechanisms:
Cellular senescence
— senolytics that clear "zombie" cells which stop dividing but refuse to die, sitting in tissue leaking inflammatory signals
Epigenetic reprogramming
— partially resetting the chemical marks on DNA that drift with age, restoring youthful gene expression without erasing cell identity
"Inflammaging"
— the chronic low-grade systemic inflammation that underlies a startling proportion of age-related disease
The regulatory obstacle is structural: the FDA does not recognize "aging" as an indication. You cannot get a drug approved to treat being old. But the workaround is already visible — surrogate composite endpoints capturing metabolic and neurocognitive health, quietly paving a path for geroprotective drugs to reach approval under other names.
You probably won't live to 150. You may well spend your seventies and eighties in meaningfully better shape than your grandparents did. That's not the headline the longevity industry wants. It's the one the data supports, and it's worth an enormous amount.
Fluorescence image of a dense network of brain cells radiating from a bright cluster
The real target of the next twenty years isn't more years. It's better ones — the biology of aging itself, attacked through senescence, epigenetic reprogramming, and chronic inflammation. (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY)
The Irony at the Center
Here's where the two halves of this story collide.
The tools of modern drug discovery — foundation models, synthetic control arms, multi-omics analysis — share a single characteristic that determines everything about their future: they are
data-hungry
. Ravenously so. A model trained on one population's genetics produces medicine that works well for that population and less well for everyone else. A synthetic control arm built from one country's health records generalizes exactly as far as that country's population does.
These systems require the diverse genetic and clinical data that only a genuinely global population can supply. That is not an ideological preference. It is a technical requirement, as hard as any constraint in the system.
And at precisely the moment when AI dissolved the boundaries between physics, chemistry, and biology — when a protein-folding model and a language model turned out to be the same kind of object, when a chemist and a machine learning engineer started working on the same problem — geopolitics began erecting walls between the people holding the tools.
BIOSECURE is one wall. There will be reciprocal walls; there already are. Data localization laws, export controls on scientific instruments, restrictions on cross-border clinical trial hosting. Each is individually defensible on national security grounds. Collectively they threaten to balkanize the one thing that made the last five years of progress possible: the free movement of biological data.
And notice where the walls fall. The discovery layer and the translation layer — the labs that find new biology and the machinery that turns it into medicine at speed — currently sit on opposite sides of the new border. Neither half is self-sufficient. A Western discovery that can't get to a clinical readout for a decade helps nobody, and a Chinese development engine with nothing novel to develop eventually runs out of road. Decoupling them doesn't produce two competing systems. It produces two incomplete ones.
If genomic datasets are confined by national borders, and manufacturing chains are weaponized for political leverage, the pace of life-saving innovation slows. Not stops — slows. And in a field where the unit of measurement is patient-years, slowing is not an abstraction. It's a body count.
There are counterweights, and they deserve more attention than they get. The
Open Discovery Innovation Network
in Europe fosters patent-free collaborative research between universities and pharmaceutical companies — pre-competitive work where nobody owns the output and everybody benefits from it existing. The Open Source Pharma Foundation is building similar scaffolding. The R Consortium's regulatory work proves that open tools can meet the most demanding standards of reproducibility in any industry.
These are small compared to the forces pushing the other way. They are also, at the moment, the best blueprint anyone has.
The science has arrived. We can now design a molecule to specification and watch it work in a human lung. We can delete a mutated protein instead of merely blocking it. We can engineer a molecule that grabs two targets at once and outperform the best cancer drug in the world — on the endpoint we measured first, at least, which is its own kind of lesson. We can forecast a patient's disease trajectory well enough to shrink the number of people who have to take the placebo.
The century-long era of guessing is genuinely over, and what replaced it is astonishing.
Whether that astonishment reaches patients is no longer a scientific question. It's a political one. And the people who will decide it mostly don't work in labs.

Drugs & Therapies.url_match_title: Why clinical trials matter: Revolutionary new kidney treatments show what UAB can deliver for Alabama patients - The University of Alabama at Birmingham
Drugs & Therapies.content:
Within the past three years, four pivotal clinical trials co-led by UAB’s Dana Rizk, M.D., have completely changed the treatment landscape for IgA nephropathy.
For decades, being diagnosed with the autoimmune kidney disease IgA (Immunoglobulin A) nephropathy carried a guarded prognosis. Most patients are young adults when they learn they have the disease, and doctors would tell them that there were few good treatment options. Often, patients would try and fail steroid therapy and other immunosuppressors.
“Here you are in the prime of your life, your 20s and 30s, and you are told that you have a chronic progressive disease which means you will likely need dialysis within your lifetime,” said Dana Rizk, M.D., professor in the
University of Alabama at Birmingham
’s
Division of Nephrology
and an expert in IgA nephropathy.
But just within the past three years, four pivotal clinical trials, co-led by Rizk, have completely changed the treatment landscape. “I am privileged and lucky to be here and live through this revolution,” Rizk said.
Based on those trial results, three separate treatments, each with a different mechanism of action, have received approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. “It is a wonderful feeling to be able to see a patient in clinic and say, ‘We have several treatment options for you,’” Rizk said. “And if one doesn’t work, we have alternatives.”
IgA nephropathy occurs when the body generates circulating immune complexes that get trapped in the kidney’s filtering units, called glomeruli, leading to inflammation and tissue damage. Symptoms, including blood and protein in the urine, can take years to develop; by the time the disease is recognized, significant damage has often occurred and patients have lost precious filtering function. IgA nephropathy is the most common of a number of rare kidney diseases, affecting around 200,000 people in the United States and millions worldwide.
These new treatments are not cures, but pushing back disease progression can be life-changing, Rizk explains. “Delaying dialysis by 10 or 20 years would have a huge effect on patients and the healthcare system,” she said.
What changed? Research and the National Kidney Initiative partnership
Years of basic research identified the molecular pathways behind IgA nephropathy. Faculty at UAB contributed significantly to these scientific advances through years of collaborations between Jan Novak, Ph.D., in the
Department of Microbiology
and Bruce Julian, M.D., and Rizk in the Division of Nephrology.
These discoveries gave pharmaceutical companies new targets for developing treatments.
But just as important, Rizk says, was an unprecedented partnership between the FDA and the American Society of Nephrology, known as the Kidney Health Initiative, meant to promote collaboration to advance education and research in nephrology.
Dana Rizk, M.D.
“Traditional clinical trials relied on ‘hard endpoints’ as the outcome of a trial: going on dialysis, receiving a kidney transplant or death,” Rizk said. That meant trials took years, enrolling patients was difficult, and pharmaceutical companies had little incentive to risk the investment in experimental therapies that might fail. The Kidney Health Initiative chose IgA nephropathy to test a new trial design and approval pathway in nephrology. “In that framework, reduction in proteinuria — protein in the urine — of a sufficient magnitude would be an acceptable surrogate trial goal,” Rizk said.
The FDA agreed to grant investigational drugs accelerated approval based on this intermediate outcome while expecting the trials to continue and confirm preservation of kidney function. At that point, the investigational drug would be granted full approval.
“That opened the door to a tremendous amount of activity and investment,” Rizk said.
Three major trials, three major successes
Rizk’s years of experience in leading and coordinating trials in rare kidney diseases, along with UAB’s pioneering role in IgA nephropathy research and clinical care, made her a go-to partner for pharmaceutical companies developing innovative drugs. Between 2024 and 2026, Rizk has been a principal investigator and steering committee member for three pivotal Phase 3 trials: APPLAUSE-IgAN, VISIONARY and ORIGIN 3. The work has led to multiple papers in the New England Journal of Medicine co-written by Rizk and accelerated FDA approval for each of these treatments.
Iptacopan
, known as Fabhalta (APPLAUSE-IgAN trial), inhibits the immune system’s alternative complement pathway. It led to significant proteinuria reduction of 38.3 percent and cut kidney function loss per year roughly in half. Fabhalta received accelerated FDA approval in 2024.
Sibeprenlimab-szsi
, known as Voyxact (VISIONARY trial), is the first approved therapy to target APRIL, a protein that interferes with production of IgA by B cells. It reduced proteinuria by about 50 percent, compared with a 2 percent rate for patients receiving placebo. Voyxact received accelerated FDA approval in November 2025.
Atacicept
(ORIGIN 3 trial), known as Trutakna, targets APRIL and BAFF, two proteins that affect a broader population of B cells, and is also expected to reduce the production of IgA. It has also shown significant proteinuria reduction of 45.7 percent from baseline and received accelerated FDA approval in July 2026.
Combined, these results signal not just new therapies but an entirely new era in the treatment for IgA nephropathy. The next steps are to test them in patients earlier in the disease course, and in pediatric patients, who have no good treatment options currently, Rizk says. New trials are also exploring the potential to treat other kidney diseases, and even other autoimmune conditions, with these new drugs.
“As a community in the IgA nephropathy space, we completely upended the clinical trial models, and now people are looking to apply this same model to other rare kidney diseases,” Rizk said. “It tells them we don’t have to have the traditional trials design we have had for the past 20 years.”
Changing people’s lives
These treatments are already making a difference for patients in the Glomerular Disease Clinic that Rizk directs at UAB. “We have changed people’s lives by giving them these therapies,” she said. “I prescribe them in the clinic and have seen the benefits firsthand. Many of the patients who took part in the trials here had tried and failed many other treatments. To know that they now have these new drugs available to them is remarkable.”
Patients with IgA nephropathy come to UAB not only from across Alabama, but from neighboring states as well, Rizk says, and the ability to participate in clinical trials is one major reason they choose to make the trip. “Offering hope for patients is probably the most important thing we do day in and day out,” Rizk said.
Developing a new generation of clinical trialists
Rizk also believes that the successes in IgA nephropathy could inspire more young clinician-scientists to become involved in clinical trials work. “For years, the nephrology space really lagged behind when it came to trials,” Rizk said. “There were huge challenges in recruiting. But these trial successes have opened the door for a whole new world and excitement in the specialty, and hopefully we will engage younger physicians in carrying on this work.”
For more than a decade, in addition to her own trials efforts, Rizk has been leading efforts to encourage younger colleagues to become clinical trialists. In 2025, she was named associate dean for Clinical Trials in the UAB
Heersink School of Medicine
. And in 2026, she co-led UAB’s new
Clinical Trialist Development Program
, a key part of the university’s
Research Strategic Initiative
, along with another renowned physician-trialist, David Kimberlin, M.D.
The goal of the Clinical Trialist Development Program is to increase the number of industry-sponsored clinical trials at UAB — and thereby the number of potential new therapies offered to Alabama patients — by expanding the university’s roster of trialists.
In modern medicine especially, clinician-researchers with expertise in rare conditions or understudied areas are highly sought after by pharmaceutical companies looking for the next IgA nephropathy-style revolution.
“These programs we are creating will foster the next generation of clinical trialists,” Rizk said.

Drugs & Therapies.url_match_title: Gibson Oncology Announces First Patient Completes Initial Treatment Cycle in Phase II Trial of LMP744 for Recurrent Glioblastoma - The Manila Times
Drugs & Therapies.content:
Novel Blood-Brain-Barrier-Penetrant Agent Being Evaluated as a Single Therapy in a Trial Conducted by the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS)
MIAMI, Aug. 11, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) --
Gibson Oncology
, a clinical-stage oncology company developing blood-brain-barrier-penetrant therapies for brain tumors and other difficult-to-treat cancers, today announced that the first patient in the Phase II clinical trial of LMP744 has been enrolled and has completed the initial treatment cycle without complication. The trial is being conducted by investigators at the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS), part of the National Institutes of Health, and is evaluating LMP744 as a single agent in patients with recurrent glioblastoma (GBM). Gibson Oncology is providing partial funding and LMP744 to the trial under a Clinical Cooperative Research and Development Agreement (CRADA) with NINDS.
LMP744 is a novel, dual-acting anticancer agent that works by reducing overexpression of the cMyc oncogene and by inhibiting topoisomerase 1 (TOPO1), two validated targets across a range of solid and hematological cancers.
Glioblastoma is the most common and aggressive primary brain tumor in adults. Approximately 13,000 new cases are diagnosed in the United States each year, median survival is generally 15 to 18 months, and the five-year survival rate is under 10 percent. Recurrent glioblastoma, for which there is no established standard of care, carries an especially poor prognosis.
In preclinical studies, LMP744 crossed the blood-brain barrier and achieved brain concentrations approximately 10 times the level needed to kill cancer cells, with a half-life in the brain exceeding 24 hours for each dose. Blood-brain-barrier penetration has long been one of the central obstacles in the treatment of brain tumors.

delivered to your inbox
Sign up for The Manila Times newsletters
By signing up with an email address, I acknowledge that I have read and agree to the
Terms of Service

Privacy Policy
.
The Phase II trial is designed to enroll a total of 40 first-time recurrent GBM patients with a Karnofsky Performance Status (KPS) of 60 or better, with a primary endpoint of progression-free survival and a secondary endpoint of overall survival. LMP744 is being studied as a single therapeutic agent based on the strong anticancer effects observed in GBM patient-derived xenograft (PDX) animal models.
LMP744 has previously completed one Phase I clinical trial with 36 patients in heavily pretreated cancer patients, many of whom had failed as many as eight prior individual or combination treatments. Over 30% of the patients on single agent treatment with LMP744 experienced stable disease for up to 30 months and 2 patients were partial responders, even as many patients were sub-optimally dosed to establish the drug’s safety and tolerability before reaching the therapeutic dose level of 190 mg/m2.

"Completing the first treatment cycle in this trial is an important early milestone for LMP744 and, most of all, for the patients who face recurrent glioblastoma with limited therapeutic options, and one of the most difficult cancers in medicine," said Randall Riggs, President and Chief Executive Officer of Gibson Oncology. "We are grateful to the clinical team at NINDS and to the patients and families taking part in this study, and we look forward to advancing LMP744 as a potential breakthrough treatment in an area that has experienced little improvement in treatment options for decades.”
Mr. Riggs continued, "The renewed excitement about LMP744 is two-fold. First, LMP744 was found to migrate rapidly into the brain at high concentrations, well beyond the levels needed to kill cancer, with each dose having a half-life of over 24 hours. Second, in PDX animal models implanted with patient-derived recurrent gliomas, just five doses of LMP744 produced tumor eradication. Together, these findings made a compelling case for initiating this Phase II study at the NINDS.”
About LMP744
LMP744 is a novel, dual-acting indenoisoquinoline that reduces cMyc overexpression and inhibits topoisomerase 1 (TOPO1). In preclinical studies, it has demonstrated blood-brain-barrier penetration and sustained brain exposure. LMP744 has been granted Orphan Drug Designation by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for all gliomas, including DIPG.
Advertisement
About Gibson Oncology
Gibson Oncology is a clinical-stage oncology company developing a portfolio of blood-brain-barrier-penetrant therapies for brain tumors and other central nervous system cancers, guided by the mission "Tough on cancer. Not on patients." The company’s lead candidates, LMP744 and LMP400, together with a next-generation series of Aza compounds, target cancers that overexpress TOPO1 and the cMyc oncogene. Based on strong preclinical data in PDX animal models with Grade 3 and Grade 4 astrocytomas resistant to standard of care, LMP400 is being developed for treating those Grade 3 and Grade 4 cancer patients who fail standard of care. Gibson Oncology holds Orphan Drug Designation for all gliomas, including DIPG, and Rare Pediatric Disease Designation for Ewing sarcoma. For more information, visit gibsononcology.com.

Pharma Industry.url_match_title: Voyageur Pharmaceuticals Advances Bayer Collaboration and Critical Minerals in the American Pharmaceutical Industry - InvestorNews
Pharma Industry.content:
When investors discuss critical minerals, they usually think about defense, energy and advanced manufacturing. Less attention is paid to the minerals required by the pharmaceutical industry, even when their availability directly affects whether hospitals can perform essential diagnostic procedures.
That is what makes
Voyageur Pharmaceuticals Ltd.
(TSXV: VM | OTC Pink: VYYRF) an unusual critical minerals story. The company’s “From Earth to Bottle” strategy is designed to control the supply chain for barium and iodine from the original resource through processing and into finished medical imaging contrast drugs.
During our August 6th interview, President, CEO and Director Brent Willis provided an update on Voyageur’s collaboration with Bayer, its Mueller iodine extraction technology, the Frances Creek barite project and plans for an integrated U.S. contrast media manufacturing facility.
“Things are proceeding very well with Bayer. “…we just completed our work plan with Bayer. So, they’ve approved it, and we’re moving forward with getting the next tranche of $1 million to come in to fund the project,” Willis said.
Under the collaboration agreement, Bayer may provide Voyageur with up to US$2.35 million in milestone-based funding for feasibility work on a proposed iodine extraction and production facility in Oklahoma. Voyageur has also
engaged
Fluor Corporation to complete feasibility studies on the Bayer iodine project and the company’s planned integrated barium and iodine contrast drug manufacturing facility.
Voyageur has established a laboratory and fabrication site in Houston to advance the Mueller Process using iodine-rich oilfield brines. Four days after our interview, the company
reported
iodine purity of 99.8% and overall recovery exceeding 90% in laboratory testing. A mobile pilot unit capable of treating approximately 80,000 litres of brine per day has been built, with field testing planned for September 2026.
“That’s going to allow Fluor Engineering to accumulate the data they require to scale up and complete our feasibility study for the projects,” Willis explained.
The Bayer project is only one part of the Voyageur strategy. The company owns 100% of the Frances Creek barite project in British Columbia and has developed five barium contrast products licensed by Health Canada. Barite remains on the
2025 U.S. List of Critical Minerals
, where its role in medical imaging is specifically recognized.
“And so, having our own barium resource that’s pharmaceutical grade in the ground gives us a significant advantage in cost savings and supply chain security and allows us to be the only producer of barium contrast in North America with our own source at very low costs and secure supply chain,” Willis said.
The iodine market carries similar supply chain risks. Willis pointed to the pandemic era shutdown of GE HealthCare’s Shanghai contrast media facility as an example of how concentrated production can affect North American hospitals.
“So, when we looked at what happened in COVID on the iodine drug side, the United States lost 50% of their supply because GE had to shut a plant down in Shanghai, China.”
Voyageur is also preparing to file a patent covering its Streamline iodine drug manufacturing process. Willis said the company believes the process could materially reduce the cost of manufacturing iodinated contrast drugs.
“We’re going to file a patent on what we call our Streamline iodine drug process. So, we have a new method of producing iodine drugs where we believe we’re going to cut the cost 50% lower than our competitors, which is going to give us a huge advantage on our marketing and market growth into the iodine space.”
Investors now have several identifiable milestones to watch: field testing of the Mueller Process, the next Bayer funding tranche, a potential Frances Creek pre-feasibility study, the Streamline patent filing, selection of a U.S. manufacturing location and completion of the Fluor-led feasibility studies in the first half of 2027.
If Voyageur can connect those pieces, “From Earth to Bottle” will describe more than a corporate strategy. It will represent a North American supply chain that links critical minerals directly to essential medical imaging drugs.

Pharma Industry.content:
View original image
AD Biotech (179530) is reinforcing its management foundation for business expansion by appointing new board members who are experts in investment, global management, law, and pharmaceuticals.
AD Biotech announced on August 11 that all agenda items to appoint two new inside directors and two new independent directors were approved as originally proposed at its general shareholders’ meeting held on the same day. The newly appointed board members are inside directors Hwang Manhoe and An Mansoo, and independent directors Lim Taehyeok and Jang Kiho.
The company explained that this board restructuring aims to enhance its capabilities in investment and management while also securing expertise in global business, law, and the pharmaceutical sector. Based on this, AD Biotech plans to further advance its existing immuno-antibody technology and accelerate the expansion of new businesses and overseas markets.
Inside director Hwang Manhoe previously served as Head of Strategic Planning at Paratech and as CEO of TSI Investment. He is expected to leverage his experience in investment and strategic planning to assist in establishing AD Biotech's mid- to long-term growth strategies, attracting investments, and enhancing management efficiency.
Inside director An Mansoo is a management expert who has served as Head of Division at Osung LST, head of Dasan Vietnam branch, and CEO of Korea Topron. The company expects that, based on his extensive domestic and international business experience, he will contribute to strengthening AD Biotech’s global business expansion, enhancing its network, and improving its management and operational processes.
Expertise in the legal sector has also been newly added to the board. Independent director Lim Taehyeok is currently a partner attorney at Yujun Law Firm. He also has experience in legislative work in the logistics and transportation sector as a national legislative advisor at the Korea Legislation Research Institute.
AD Biotech plans to utilize Lim's legal expertise to proactively respond to potential legal risks that may arise during business expansion and to strengthen its compliance and legal management systems.
Independent director Jang Kiho previously worked as a researcher at Whanin Pharmaceutical, was CEO of Daehak Pharmacy, and is currently CEO of Jeongmun Daehak Pharmacy. Based on his experience accumulated in the pharmaceutical and pharmacy sectors, he is expected to provide expertise in bio-pharmaceutical R&D and the promotion of new healthcare businesses.
Leveraging the new board structure, AD Biotech aims to fortify its business competitiveness using its existing immuno-antibody technology, while also entering new business fields such as digital healthcare.
In particular, the company believes that securing expertise in diverse fields such as investment and strategic planning, global management, law, and pharmaceuticals on the board will enhance decision-making capabilities for business diversification and global market expansion.

LG CNS Builds AI Drug Discovery Platform for Dong-A Socio Group, Accelerating Pharma AX Business
Add to Google Preferred Sources
LG CNS, in collaboration with DAI — the IT affiliate of Dong-A Socio Group — has completed an AI-powered drug discovery platform after approximately six months of development. The platform integrates and standardizes previously scattered drug research data, leveraging AI to support the entire drug development lifecycle, from candidate compound identification and molecular design to virtual validation. A key feature is its continuous learning architecture: AI predictions are iteratively cross-referenced with actual experimental results, meaning predictive accuracy improves as research progresses. Building on this project, along with prior work for Chong Kun Dang and a project under South Korea's Ministry of Health and Welfare, LG CNS plans to aggressively expand its pharmaceutical and biotech AI transformation (AX) business by integrating its specialized agentic AI platform.
Key Elements
LG CNS
Dong-A Socio Group
DAI
AI Drug Discovery Platform
Lee Jae-seung
AgenticWorks for BIO
Chong Kun Dang
South Korea's Ministry of Health and Welfare
LG CNS announced on August 12 that it has built an 'AI Drug Discovery Platform' in partnership with DAI, the IT services arm of Dong-A Socio Group. The core objective of the roughly six-month project was to deploy AI across the entire drug development process, from integrating and standardizing research data to candidate compound discovery, molecular design, and virtual validation.
Drug development, which typically takes 10 to 15 years, requires massive investment and time due to the need for repetitive validation of countless candidate compounds. LG CNS explained that AI can rapidly filter for high-probability candidates and predict efficacy and safety profiles in advance, simultaneously reducing development timelines, costs, and the risk of failure.
During the platform's construction, LG CNS consolidated and standardized drug research data that had been scattered across disparate sources, including information on chemical compounds, genomic data, experimental results, academic papers, and patents. Researchers can now query necessary data on a single platform and utilize AI analysis and prediction features with just a few clicks.
The platform offers AI functions optimized for each stage of drug development. In the disease target identification phase, AI analyzes and visualizes cell-specific genetic information and spatial tissue data to help researchers easily pinpoint therapeutic targets. During the candidate design phase, generative AI directly creates novel molecular structures based on conditions set by the researcher. In the validation phase, the platform simulates binding affinity between candidates and targets, as well as interaction stability, allowing promising compounds to be prioritized before physical experiments begin.
A particularly noteworthy aspect is the AI model's continuous performance improvement mechanism. By comparing AI-generated predictions with actual experimental data and feeding the results back into model retraining, predictive accuracy is progressively enhanced as research data accumulates. LG CNS designed the system to organically link the entire workflow — from data collection and AI analysis to experimentation and validation — boosting the speed and quality of drug discovery while ensuring that accumulated research data becomes a valuable future asset. Given the sensitive nature of drug research data, the company also established a management framework to comply with pharmaceutical industry regulations and security requirements.
This platform build leverages LG CNS's accumulated capabilities in AI transformation (AX) for the pharmaceutical and biotech sectors. The company previously participated in South Korea's Ministry of Health and Welfare's 'K-AI Drug Discovery Preclinical and Clinical Model Development R&D Project' and developed an 'Agentic AI-based Annual Quality Review Report Service' for Chong Kun Dang. Recently, LG CNS has been expanding its business in both public and private markets with 'AgenticWorks for BIO,' an agentic AI platform specialized for the pharmaceutical and biotech industry.
"Through differentiated AX technologies, including agentic AI, and our specialized expertise in the pharmaceutical and biotech fields, we will contribute to innovation in AI-driven drug research and development within South Korea's pharmaceutical and biotech industry," said Lee Jae-seung, Managing Director of LG CNS's Cloud Business Division. "We will actively support our clients in strengthening their drug development competitiveness."

Pharma Industry.content:
Baihua Pharma Flags No Innovative Drug R&D After Six-Day Winning Streak, PE Ratio 5x Industry Average
Add to Google Preferred Sources
After six consecutive trading days of hitting the upper limit and a 77% surge during the period, Baihua Pharmaceutical issued a statement clarifying that it is a CRO focused primarily on small-molecule generic chemical drug R&D and is not involved in innovative drug development. The company's Q1 2026 revenue fell 30.68% year-on-year, with net profit down 67.94%, yet its latest trailing PE ratio has soared to 184.25x—more than five times the industry average of 34.96x. The company used unusually blunt language, including "a clear pass-the-parcel effect," to warn of overheated market sentiment and irrational speculation, stating the stock price has severely deviated from fundamentals. On the same day, China's A-share innovative drug concept stocks broadly rallied, with Wanbang Pharmaceutical, Yatai Group, and Gan & Lee Pharmaceuticals all hitting their daily upper limits.
Key Elements
Baihua Pharmaceutical
600721.SH
CRO
innovative drugs
Wanbang Pharmaceutical
Gan & Lee Pharmaceuticals
Yatai Group
Against the backdrop of a sustained rally in China's A-share innovative drug concept stocks, Baihua Pharmaceutical (600721.SH) has captured the market's spotlight with a blistering six consecutive trading days of hitting the daily upper limit. However, as its share price rocketed higher, the company's own announcement disclosed on the evening of August 11 poured cold water on the frenzy: Baihua explicitly stated it is not involved in innovative drug R&D, its valuation metrics have significantly exceeded the industry average, and the cumulative share price surge has severely deviated from fundamentals.
As of the close on August 11, Baihua Pharmaceutical hit its upper limit again, closing at 12.75 yuan per share, officially notching a six-day winning streak. According to the company's announcement, its share price surged 77.07% between August 4 and August 11. This staggering short-term gain not only far outpaced the broader market during the same period but also significantly outperformed its sector index.
Confronted with the unusual share price movement, Baihua Pharmaceutical used unusually blunt language in its announcement, including phrases like "a clear pass-the-parcel effect," warning of the risks of overheated sentiment and irrational speculation. The company directly pointed out that its core business is as a CRO (Contract Research Organization) primarily focused on small-molecule generic chemical drug R&D. As of now, its main business has not undergone material changes and does not involve the innovative drug R&D that the market is currently speculating on.
The Divergence Between Fundamentals and Share Price
In stark contrast to the red-hot share price, Baihua Pharmaceutical's operating data appears somewhat lackluster. The company's previously disclosed Q1 2026 report showed quarterly revenue of 67.18 million yuan (approximately $10.0 million), down 30.68% year-on-year. Net profit attributable to shareholders of the listed company was just 6.64 million yuan (approximately $986,530), a sharp year-on-year decline of 67.94%. The company emphasized in its announcement that fundamentals have not undergone material changes, nor have there been significant adjustments to the market environment or industry policies.
The divergence at the valuation level is even more pronounced. As of the announcement date, Baihua Pharmaceutical's latest trailing price-to-earnings ratio had soared to 184.25x. According to data provided by the company, the trailing PE ratio for its industry is just 34.96x. This means Baihua Pharmaceutical's valuation level is more than five times the industry average.
Collective Frenzy in the Innovative Drug Sector
Baihua Pharmaceutical's surge is not an isolated case. Behind it lies a collective burst of activity across the entire A-share innovative drug sector since August. On August 11 alone, the innovative drug concept surged again. Wanbang Pharmaceutical hit its 20% daily upper limit, while Yatai Group and Gan & Lee Pharmaceuticals (603087.SH) also reached their daily trading caps.
However, Baihua Pharmaceutical's case serves as a cautionary footnote to this wave of enthusiasm. Despite being lumped into the "innovative drug concept stock" basket and chased by capital, the company's actual business substance is far removed from innovative drugs. This vast temperature gap between market perception and the company's fundamentals is precisely where risk accumulates.
Valuation Comparison and Risk Warning
Below is a valuation comparison between Baihua Pharmaceutical and the industry average, compiled from the company's announcement:

In its announcement, the company stated bluntly that the share price has risen continuously over the short term with significant short-term gains, already markedly exceeding the increases of both the sector and the Shanghai Composite Index over the same period. It directly reminded investors that "participating in trading may entail significant risks." Such a risk warning originating from the listed company itself is uncommon in the A-share market and indirectly reflects that the degree of deviation between the current share price and the company's intrinsic value may have reached a level requiring insiders to proactively speak out.
This episode of Baihua Pharmaceutical's share price anomaly and the subsequent clarifying announcement provides investors with a window to examine the current market hotspots. When the winds of concept speculation blow, the short-term profit-seeking behavior of capital can blur the true face of a listed company. Ultimately, the long-term trajectory of a stock price must return to the solid support of fundamentals.

Global Biopharmaceuticals Market Outlook
(Reference: statista.com)
In 2025, the worldwide biopharmaceuticals market is expected to reach about USD 336 billion.
By 2026, the market is projected to grow further to nearly USD 367 billion.
Looking ahead, the market size is forecast to climb steadily and could approach USD 566 billion by 2032.
Biopharmaceuticals Market by Product Type
(Source: coherentmarketinsights.com)
In 2026, the global biopharmaceuticals market is led by monoclonal antibodies with a 36.5% share.
Vaccines represent 15.5%, while recombinant proteins account for 9.5% and recombinant hormones hold 8.9%.
Cell and
gene therapies
, recombinant growth factors, and purified proteins contribute 7.9%, 6.3%, and 5.5%, respectively.
Synthetic immunomodulators, recombinant enzymes, and other product types together comprise the remaining 4.5%.
By Therapeutic Application
(Source: coherentmarketinsights.com)
Oncology holds the largest share at 25%, confirming cancer as the primary focus area for biopharmaceutical development.
Inflammatory and infectious diseases follow at 17%, while autoimmune disorders represent 13%.
Hormonal disorders and metabolic disorders account for 11% and 10%, respectively.
Cardiovascular diseases account for 9%, neurological diseases for 8%, and other diseases for the remaining 7%.
Change in Biopharma Enterprise Value, 2025-2026
(Reference: statista.com)
Commercial pharma leads the sector with a 19.5% rise in enterprise value, while pharma services increase 11.9% as outsourcing and specialized support continue to grow.
API companies record an 11% gain, reflecting stable upstream demand, while CDMOs post a 4.4% increase through steady project growth.
Biotech declines 5.1% as investors remain cautious about early-stage assets, while OTC medicines fall 6.5% because of margin pressure and strong retail competition.
Biopharma Enterprise Value by Subsector
(Reference: statista.com)
In February 2026, commercial pharma dominated biopharma, with enterprise value around USD 7,379,391 million.
Biotech and pharma services were mid‑sized contributors, at USD 407,030 million and USD 192,611 million, respectively.
Meanwhile, contract development and manufacturing organizations captured around USD 162,241 million, and active pharmaceutical ingredients made up USD 99,901 million.
Over‑the‑counter medicines remained a smaller segment, with an enterprise value of USD 22,425 million.

Leading Global Biopharmaceutical Companies Statistics
(Source: pharmashots.com)
Eli Lilly and Company (Lilly)
Total revenue reached USD 65.17B in 2025. The company was founded in 1876, employs 50,000 people, is headquartered in Indiana, United States, has a USD 902.48B market cap, and is listed on the NYSE.
Lilly focuses on diabetes, obesity, oncology, immunology, and neuroscience. Revenue increased 44.7% YoY, led by Mounjaro (USD 22.96B), Zepbound (USD 13.54B), and Verzenio (USD 5.72B).
In Apr. 2026, the US FDA approved Foundayo (Orforglipron) for weight loss.
Pfizer
Pfizer
generated USD 61.19B in revenue in 2025. Founded in 1849, it has 75,000 employees, is based in New York, United States, has a USD 154.84B market cap, and trades on the NYSE.
The company develops vaccines, oncology, cardiology, and rare disease treatments. Revenue declined 1.92% YoY, while Eliquis (USD 7.9B), Prevnar (USD 6.4B), and Vyndaqel (USD 6.38B) remained key products.
In Feb. 2026, the US FDA fully approved the Braftovi regimen for metastatic colorectal cancer.
AbbVie
AbbVie reported USD 61.16B in revenue. Founded in 2013, it employs 57,000 people, is headquartered in Illinois, United States, has a USD 375.69B market cap, and is listed on the NYSE.
Revenue grew 8.56% YoY, supported by Skyrizi (USD 17.56B), Rinvoq (USD 8.3B), and Humira (USD 4.54B).
In Jan. 2026, AbbVie signed an approximately USD 5.6B deal with Remegen for RC148.
Johnson & Johnson (J&J)
J&J
recorded USD 60.4B in revenue. Founded in 1886, it has 138,200 employees, is headquartered in New Jersey, United States, has a USD 581.22B market cap, and trades on the NYSE.
Revenue increased 6.03% YoY, driven by Darzalex (USD 14.35B), Stelara (USD 6.07B), and Tremfya (USD 5.15B).
In Jan. 2026, the US FDA approved the Darzalex FASPRO regimen for newly diagnosed multiple myeloma.
Roche
Roche
generated USD 60.34B in revenue. Founded in 1896, it employs 112,800 people, is headquartered in Basel, Switzerland, has a USD 328.89B market cap, and is listed on the SWX.
The company combines pharmaceuticals and diagnostics, with revenue rising 18.05% YoY. Its top products include Ocrevus (USD 8.87B), Hemlibra (USD 6.01B), and Vabysmo (USD 5.19B).
In Feb. 2026, the US FDA accepted Roche’s Giredestrant NDA for ESR1-mutated, ER-positive advanced breast cancer.

(Source: precedenceresearch.com)
In 2025, the AI in biopharmaceutical market is valued at about USD 1.99 billion, rising to USD 2.63 billion in 2026.
By 2030, the market is projected to reach around USD 8.07 billion, reflecting strong adoption of AI-driven drug discovery and development tools.
Looking ahead to 2035, the market is expected to scale sharply to nearly USD 29.78 billion.

artificial intelligence
in the biopharmaceutical market revenue in 2025.

By technology, natural language processing generated over 32% of revenue in 2025.
By offering, hardware led with 44% of the market.
By deployment, the
cloud segment
captured 52% of the market share in 2025.
Biopharma shareholder returns overview by Long‑term Index Performance.
(Source: web-assets.bcg.com)
Biopharma has historically delivered higher returns than the broader S&P 500, particularly during 2011-2015 when the S&P Biotech Index reached about 29%.
From 2006-2010, biopharma outperformed with nearly 8% versus roughly 5% for the S&P 500.
The return gap narrowed in 2016-2020, with biopharma at around 19% and the S&P 500 near 16%.
In 2021-2025, biopharma performance slowed further, converging toward 0-16%.
Leading Biopharma Company Returns in 2025
According to BCG, twelve of the top 20 global pharma companies delivered a one‑year total shareholder return above the S&P 500 benchmark of approximately 15%.
Top performers achieved TSRs in the range of roughly 24%-58%, reflecting successful pipelines, disciplined capital allocation, and investor confidence.
The weakest players recorded TSRs as low as about -57%.
Biopharma and Medtech Capital Markets Overview
Biopharma and medtech capital markets started 2026 on a stable note, with investors focusing on later-stage assets and well-established programs.
In biopharma, licensing activity remained strong, with total announced R&D deal value reaching USD 166.7 billion in H1 2026, while upfront payments accounted for 6% of total deal value, according to a report shared by JP Morgan.
Biopharma M&A reached USD 96 billion across 80 deals, including USD 55.1 billion from 48 deals in Q2 2026.
Venture funding totaled USD 16.3 billion across 235 rounds, while 13 IPOs raised USD 5.0 billion, exceeding every full-year total recorded between 2022 and 2025.
In medtech, M&A reached USD 48.9 billion across 92 deals, including USD 22.3 billion from 47 deals in Q2 2026.
Medtech venture funding totaled USD 5.0 billion across 164 rounds, while 2 IPOs raised USD 710 million. Licensing generated USD 5.8 billion, with only 1% paid upfront.
Product Development Updates
April 2025: NVIDIA expanded its BioNeMo generative AI platform with new foundation models for protein structure prediction, molecular generation, and AI-powered drug discovery, helping biopharmaceutical companies speed up research.
2025: Insilico Medicine advanced multiple AI-designed drug candidates into clinical development, strengthening the use of AI in biopharmaceutical R&D.
November 2025: AI-supported therapies, including DARZALEX FASPRO, KEYTRUDA QLEX, and EYLEA HD, reached commercialization, reflecting wider AI adoption in product development.
April 2026: The U.S. FDA approved Foundayo (orforglipron) in just 50 days, 294 days ahead of its PDUFA date, making it the first NME approved under the National Priority Voucher Program and the fastest approval since 2002.
May 2026: Takeda reported 3 positive Phase 3 readouts, 2 regulatory submissions, and plans for 3 major product launches within the next 12 months.
May 2026: Novo Nordisk said AI could shorten the path from late-stage trials to regulatory filing by up to two-thirds, improving development speed.
Closing
Biopharmaceuticals are changing the way many diseases are treated by offering safer and more targeted medicines. They are helping improve care for cancer, rare diseases, and many long-term health conditions. While high costs and strict regulations remain challenges, new research and better technology continue to drive growth.
As more innovative treatments become available, biopharmaceuticals will play a bigger role in improving healthcare, giving patients better treatment options, and supporting longer, healthier lives.
FAQ
How are biopharmaceuticals different from traditional medicines?
Biopharmaceuticals are made from living cells using biotechnology, while traditional medicines are chemically manufactured using synthetic ingredients and processes.
What diseases can biopharmaceuticals treat?
Biopharmaceuticals treat cancer, diabetes, autoimmune disorders, infections, rare diseases, and genetic conditions.
How are biopharmaceuticals manufactured?
Biopharmaceuticals are made by genetically engineered living cells, then purified, tested, and packaged for medical use.

Pharma Industry.url_match_title: Kolon Pharma spins off drug R&D unit to launch TonX BIO - koreabiomed.com
Pharma Industry.content:
Kolon Pharma is spinning off its drug development business to establish TonX BIO (pronounced "T-on-X Bio"), returning to an independent management structure three years after absorbing oncology drug developer FlatBio to bring its R&D capabilities in-house.
The new company will be headed by Kim Sun-jin, founder of FlatBio and former head of Kolon Pharma’s drug development division.
Using the research personnel and drug pipelines that joined Kolon Pharma through the FlatBio merger, TonX BIO plans to pursue independent drug development with translational research as its core competency.
In a public disclosure last Friday, Kolon Pharma said it will establish TonX BIO through a spin-off of its drug development division. The surviving company, Kolon Pharma, will focus on pharmaceutical manufacturing and sales, while the new company will focus on drug research and development.
Kolon Pharma said the split aims to strengthen specialization in each business.
Under the plan, Kolon Pharma will focus on stable operations and improving profitability in its existing pharmaceutical business. TonX BIO will establish an independent management structure dedicated to new drug development, strengthening its R&D capabilities and specialized decision-making.
TonX BIO will be headed by Kim Sun-jin, founder of FlatBio and former head of Kolon Pharma’s drug development division. (Produced by KBR with ChatGPT)
More than half of net assets to move to new company, along with pipelines, patents and staff
The split ratio is 0.4562548 for Kolon Pharma and 0.5437452 for TonX BIO.
As of the end of March, the net book value of Kolon Pharma’s total assets stood at approximately 71.5 billion won ($50.4 million), of which about 38.9 billion won was attributed to the drug development business. On a net asset basis, more than half of the company’s assets will be transferred to the new entity.
In addition to the assets and liabilities of the drug development business, related regulatory approvals, contracts and intellectual property rights, including patents, utility models and trademarks, will, in principle, be transferred to TonX BIO.
The new company will also assume the employment relationships and working conditions of employees assigned to the drug development business.
A shareholders’ meeting to approve the split is scheduled for Aug. 21, with Sept. 30 set as the record date for the allocation of shares in the new company. Existing shareholders will receive TonX BIO shares in proportion to their holdings as of the record date. The split will take effect Oct. 1.
The move comes just over three years after Kolon Pharma absorbed FlatBio in June 2023, effectively making its drug development operation independent again.
At the time, Kolon Pharma pursued the merger to combine its existing pharmaceutical business with FlatBio’s oncology drug development capabilities. It later adopted a co-CEO structure, with CEO Jeon Jae-kwang overseeing the pharmaceutical business and FlatBio founder Kim heading the drug development business.
Once TonX BIO launches, the drug development organization, largely built around the former FlatBio, will regain its independence.
Kolon Group also described the spin-off as a process in which FlatBio, previously an external organization, joined Kolon Pharma, after which its research personnel, patents and pipelines will now be separated into an independent company.
Kim Sun-jin returns to drug development forefront, emphasizing translational research
Kim will lead TonX BIO.
After graduating from Seoul National University College of Medicine, Kim earned a master’s degree in medicine and a doctorate in immunology from the university’s graduate school. He then spent about 19 years as a professor at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center.
After returning to Korea, he served as executive vice president in charge of R&D at Hanmi Pharmaceutical before founding FlatBio in 2018.
Kim’s ties with Kolon Group began in 2020, when he joined Kolon TissueGene as an outside director. He later served as chief medical officer of Kolon TissueGene and was appointed CEO of Kolon Life Science in 2023. That same year, when FlatBio was absorbed into Kolon Pharma, he also took charge of Kolon Pharma’s drug development division.
His drug development experience has focused particularly on oncology, including translational research and orthotopic transplantation models.
TonX BIO said the “T” in its new name, “TonX,” represents “Translational Research,” which the company identifies as its core competency. The name reflects its goal of increasing the likelihood of clinical success for its proprietary drug pipelines and translating them into therapeutic solutions for patients.
The “X” represents three growth strategies: “NEXT GENERATION (neXt),” referring to next-generation therapeutics; “COLLABORATION (Cross),” representing joint research with pharmaceutical and biotech companies and research institutions; and “OUR Platform (eXpertise),” referring to its proprietary platform technologies and expertise.
The company plans to expand collaborative research with other companies and research institutions while advancing its own platform technologies, aiming to become “a global company leading the development of next-generation oncology drugs” based on translational research.
The spin-off will once again place Kolon Pharma’s pharmaceutical and drug development businesses under separate management structures.
Kolon Pharma will focus on improving the profitability and competitiveness of its existing pharmaceutical operations, while TonX BIO will concentrate its resources on advancing its drug pipelines under an independent decision-making structure.
The key question will be whether TonX BIO can turn the translational research capabilities and drug pipelines inherited from the FlatBio era into tangible development results.
Having opted for independent management again following the 2023 merger with Kolon Pharma, TonX BIO will now seek to advance its drug candidates and pursue licensing deals and joint development partnerships under Kim’s leadership.

Pharma Industry.url_match_title: BlackRock boosts stakes in Korea biotech, betting on long-term growth - CHOSUNBIZ - Chosunbiz
Pharma Industry.content: BlackRock, the world’s largest asset manager, has been snapping up shares of Korea’s bio corporations in quick succession. Following HLB(028300), it has aggressively increased its equity in Alteogen(196170) and Yuhan(000100), prompting analysis that this is more than simple bargain hunting and reflects a high assessment of the growth potential of Korea’s pharmaceutical and biotech industry. According to the industry on the 12th, BlackRock Fund Advisors, which manages BlackRock’s funds, and its special affiliates bought 745,717 shares of Yuhan on the market through the 31st of last month. As a result, BlackRock’s Yuhan holdings increased from 4,039,408 shares to 4,785,125 shares. Its equity stake also rose 1.43 percentage points, from 5.07% to 6.50%. This follows a move in June to raise its stake from 4.36% to 5.07%, expanding its investment weight for the second consecutive month. Yuhan is expected to see improved profitability as global sales of the lung cancer drug “Leclaza (ingredient name Lazertinib)” expand. As Leclaza’s global sales increase, revenue from milestone payments and royalties tied to sales is also projected to grow. BlackRock has also expanded its investment in Alteogen. On the 31st of last month, it bought an additional 24,273 shares of Alteogen, raising its equity stake from 4.98% to 5.03%. Alteogen’s core technology is the hyaluronidase platform “ALT-B4,” which converts intravenous (IV) formulations into subcutaneous (SC) formulations. In January, it signed a 420 billion won deal with Tesaro Inc., a subsidiary of GSK plc in the United Kingdom, and in March it signed an 867.5 billion won deal with U.S.-based Biogen. Early this month, it also clinched a technology out-licensing deal worth around 500 billion won with a global pharmaceutical company, continuing its run of technology export results. In particular, HLB is where BlackRock most aggressively increased its equity. After raising its HLB equity stake to 5.01% in March, BlackRock expanded it to 6.05% in June to become the second-largest shareholder after Chair Jin Yang-gon, and by the end of last month it further increased its holding to 7.15%. Notably, buying continued even after HLB received a third complete response letter (CRL) from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) regarding the combination therapy of the liver cancer drug candidate “Rivoceranib” and “Camrelizumab” from China’s Hengrui Medicine. From the 10th to the 30th of last month, after HLB disclosed on the 9th that it had received a CRL, BlackRock acquired an additional 855,814 shares of HLB. Despite a sharp drop in HLB’s share price due to the FDA approval delay, it increased its holding ratio. In the market, some interpret this as BlackRock taking a positive view of HLB’s chances for new drug approval and its long-term corporate value. However, BlackRock describes its purpose as “simple investment,” making it difficult to confirm the specific investment background. BlackRock’s investment in Korea’s biotech sector is not limited to individual corporations but is expanding across the board. As of the end of June, BlackRock held equity stakes of 5% or more in 19 listed Korean companies, up by 12 from a year earlier. Of these, four are bio-related corporations, including LG Chem(051910). Since opening its Seoul office early this year, BlackRock has been expanding its points of contact for investment in domestic corporations. The market is paying attention to the fact that global investors continue to increase their equity stakes even as Korea’s bio stocks undergo a correction. The analysis is that, beyond simple bargain hunting, they highly rate the technological competitiveness and potential for global business expansion of Korea’s bio corporations. In fact, as Korea’s pharmaceutical and biotech corporations have recently been clinching a series of technology exports, co-development deals, and partnerships with global drugmakers and expanding their presence overseas, observers say interest from foreign institutional investors is growing. Seo Geun-hee, an analyst at Samsung Securities, said, “Foreign institutional investors analyze and invest in corporations from a mid- to long-term perspective rather than seeking short-term trading gains,” and added, “Deciding to invest in domestic bio corporations regardless of current market conditions means they highly evaluate the overall growth potential of Korea’s pharmaceutical and biotech industry.” Heo Hye-min, an analyst at Kiwoom Securities, said, “The mere fact that the largest overseas asset manager is increasing its touchpoints with domestic bio corporations is a positive signal that was rare in Korea’s bio sector in the past,” and added, “Recent successive technology export results and investor relations (IR) for overseas investors by those corporations appear to have had an impact.”

Pharma Industry.url_match_title: Antibody-drug conjugates: Why it takes a village to make them - cen.acs.org
Pharma Industry.content:
Key Insights
Pharmaceutical and biotech companies are rushing to develop new generations of antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) for treating cancer.
It often takes multiple drug services firms to manufacture ADCs.
Some firms make the entire molecule; others make individual components. Experts say that there is a demand for all types of services in the ADC field.
As antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) continue to catch the fancy of the pharmaceutical and biotechnology worlds, it is becoming ever more clear that it takes a village to bring them from concept to commercial drug.
In the past year, several contract development and manufacturing organizations (CDMOs) have made hefty investments to support the rising demand for ADCs from their clients—the innovator drug companies that are designing and testing the conjugates. Only a handful of CDMOs
make ADCs from start to finish
. Many more are tailoring their services to produce the individual
nuts and bolts of ADC molecules
.
ADCs are attractive therapeutics precisely because their constituent parts can unleash attacks on cancer cells while sparing healthy ones. In a typical ADC, the drug, or payload, is a toxic small molecule that targets the cancer cell’s DNA; a monoclonal antibody serves as a vehicle to guide the payload to the tumor; and a linker connects the payload to the antibody.
But the field of ADC development is not standing still. As pharmaceutical and biotech companies deploy their research and development capital to engineer new varieties of ADCs, the CDMOs that work with them are ramping up their services in kind. As the field continues to boom, drug services firms are going to be busy for a long time.
A worker stands in white full-body protective gear in a facility with stainless steel walls.
A worker wearing protective gear at Lonza’s plant in Visp, Switzerland, that makes highly potent active pharmaceutical ingredients.
Credit:
 Lonza
ADCs are a new pharma favorite
The US Food and Drug Administration approved the first ADC in 2000 as a
treatment for a form of acute myeloid leukemia
. The molecule, called gemtuzumab ozogamicin and sold under the brand name Mylotarg, was developed by the biotech companies Wyeth and Celltech. But after nearly a decade on the market,
the drug was withdrawn
because of concerns about its safety and efficacy.
"Right now, everyone wants to be in the ADC space."
That setback didn’t stop the ADC field from flourishing. Since Mylotarg’s withdrawal, over a dozen ADCs have reached the market, including the most recent, AbbVie’s Decnupaz for treatment of a rare blood cancer. Mylotarg even returned in 2017, when the FDA approved its use at a lower dose.
According to
Hanson Wade’s Beacon platform
, which provides information on clinical trials, over 200 ADC drug candidates are being actively tested in clinical trials worldwide.
“Right now, everyone wants to be in the ADC space,” says Dowdy Jackson, founder of Jackson Consulting Group, which advises pharma and biotech companies on clinical development strategies.
Jackson says the ADC field has become crowded,and companies are trying to figure out how to stand out. “They are starting to throw everything against the wall and seeing what sticks,” he says.
Innovation is happening across all three parts of the ADC complex. For instance, companies are replacing small-molecule payloads with oligonucleotides, which act as
RNA silencers
, or with
radioactive isotopes
that deliver radiation to cancer cells. Others are rethinking antibodies by giving them more arms to bind to different parts of cancer and immune cells. And in recent years, companies, including industry giants such as
Merck & Co
., have started making
novel ADC linkers
.
The market value of those innovations is perhaps best reflected in the billions of dollars pharma companies have shelled out to acquire biotech start-ups with novel ADC technology. Already this year, at least four blockbuster deals have been signed in the ADC space.
In April, Eli Lilly and Company
agreed to acquire the early-stage ADC biotech CrossBridge Bio
, which has developed dual-payload ADCs and peptide-based linkers that can easily cleave from payloads. In June, Johnson & Johnson paid
$1 billion to acquire Firefly Bio
, a start-up focused on making degrader-antibody conjugates—molecules in which the antibodies are fused to a
targeted protein-degrader
instead of a typical small molecule. And in July, Novartis agreed to pay up to $1.5 billion for Myricx Bio, a start-up focused on a novel payload technology.
The largest deal, agreed on in April and completed a month later, saw Gilead Sciences spend $3.15 billion to
acquire Tubuilis, a German start-up.
Tubulis has novel linker technologies that ensure stable delivery of payloads to cancer cells. Among its lead candidates are molecules to treat ovarian cancer and non-small-cell lung cancer.
One-stop shops aren’t standing still
Big service firms expand to make conjugates
Lonza
Expanding payload-linker production and purification capabilities in Visp, Switzerland
Investment: Undisclosed
Year announced: 2026
Piramal Pharma Solutions
Expanding commercial-scale payload-linker sites in Riverview, Michigan, and Lexington, Kentucky
Investment: $90 million
Year announced: 2025
Veranova
Setting up a new bioconjugation facility and process development lab in Devens, Massachusetts
Investment: Over $50 million
Years announced: 2024 and 2025
Carbogen Amcis
Expanding ADC production capabilities at its sites in Switzerland
Investment: $31 million
Year announced: 2025
MilliporeSigma
Expanding to triple ADC manufacturing capacity in Saint Louis
Investment: $76 million
Year announced: 2024
While pharma and biotech companies reimagine ADCs, CDMOs skilled in manufacturing them find themselves busy.
The process of making ADCs typically involves producing the antibodies, payloads, and linkers separately and then combining them. The antibody is usually expressed in mammalian cells, while the payload and linker are synthesized via chemical processes and attached together. The payload-linker duo is then fused to the antibody via bioconjugation, and the resulting ADC is packaged into a vial or syringe under sterile conditions.
Biotech and pharmaceutical companies often hire CDMOs to manufacture the molecules for use in preclinical and clinical trials and then to make FDA-approved ADCs at commercial scale.
Lonza, the industry leader in the CDMO space, can perform all those steps in-house, given its capabilities in producing all kinds of molecules, from small molecules to large biologics. “Lonza entered the [ADC-manufacturing] space quite early, in 2006. And over time, we have tried our best to establish a full CDMO service, really covering the whole value chain,” says
Iwan Bertholjotti
, senior director of commercial development for bioconjugates at Lonza.
In 2023,
Lonza acquired Synaffix
, a biotech company that had developed three technologies for fusing payloads to linkers, for $107 million and possible milestone payments. According to Lonza’s
announcement at the time
, Synaffix’s technologies can considerably enhance the efficacy and tolerability of ADCs. And this June, Lonza announced plans to expand its payload-linker manufacturing capacity in Visp, Switzerland, to support
rapidly growing customer demand
. The company also manufactures antibodies and performs bioconjugation at the site.
Abzena also offers most of the services required to make ADCs. Like Lonza, the British firm invested in facilities needed to make ADCs in the early days, a choice that its chief scientific officer, Campbell Bunce
,
now describes as “serendipitous.”
Today, the company also has manufacturing capabilities in the US. There’s a biologics manufacturing facility in San Diego, and facilities in Bristol, Pennsylvania, where the company makes high-potency pharmaceutical ingredients for payloads and linkers and offers bioconjugation services. In 2024, Abzena
invested $5 million at the Bristol site
to ramp up bioconjugation capabilities.
The company now offers bioconjugation of next-generation ADCs that contain molecules such as antisense RNAs, protein degraders, and radioisotopes. But even one-stop shops such as Lonza and Abzena can’t do it all. For example, neither has the capability to manufacture oligonucleotides.
“We work with our client to find the best solution for that,” Bunce says. “They might have a preferred provider already, or we know groups that do that very well and can connect our client to other companies.”
Stitching ADCs piece by piece
While some CDMOs offer almost everything under one umbrella, others have clear priorities: either they offer some combination of payload, linker, and bioconjugation services or they focus on the antibody side of the ADC business. But the inability to provide end-to-end services doesn’t seem to hurt their business prospects.
Axplora, for instance, makes small-molecule active-pharmaceutical-ingredient (API) payloads and linkers and offers bioconjugation services, but it does not manufacture antibodies. Over the years, the company has added services such as linker-payload manufacturing and bioconjugation to its roster. Jin-Seok Hur, global platform head for ADCs at the firm, says small-molecule API manufacturing continues to be the company’s bread and butter.
And those services are in demand. In 2024, Axplora announced it would invest nearly $9 million to expand ADC payload manufacturing capacity in Le Mans, France. And in 2025, the company said it would further that expansion, although it did not disclose the investment amount. Axplora is also investing
$60 million
to expand production of high-potency APIs, some of which are used in ADC payloads, in Gropello Cairoli, Italy.
Hur says companies with a strong presence in biologics are the ones focused on making antibodies. “But they need someone like us, the small-molecule-based company
,
for making the linker, payload, and bioconjugation.”
Different companies, different preferences
When a drug company decides to hire multiple CDMOs to make the various parts of an ADC, it must ensure it has the human power to coordinate the various stages of drug development, Jackson, the pharma consultant, says. And most small biotech companies don’t have this luxury. “If you’re a small biotech, you really don’t have very many people. Some of them have just two or three people. Who’s going to manage all this?”
For example, the Canadian biotech Zymeworks has been developing ADCs for nearly 2 decades. The company’s commercial ADC,
Ziihera, for the treatment of biliary tract cancer
, received FDA approval in 2024. The firm has over a dozen more ADCs in various stages of clinical study.
Zymeworks outsources the manufacturing of those ADCs to the Chinese CDMO WuXi AppTec, another one-stop shop. “We don’t really use them to develop our molecules and take them forward,” says Sabeen Mekan, chief medical officer at Zymeworks. “We really use them for manufacturing.”
Bertholjotti says the one-stop-shop offerings from firms such as Lonza are appreciated most by up-and-coming biotechs and pharmaceutical companies with complex ADCs in the early stages of development.
In contrast, Bertholjotti says, large drug companies with more-standard ADCs tend to hand-pick the ADC services they need. “They may have some in-house capabilities—say, maybe they can produce the monoclonal antibodies in-house—and then they don’t need [to outsource] that piece.”
Hur agrees. “Big pharma tries to find the best in each area. So best player for antibody, best player for linker payload, best player for bioconjugation, and best player for fill and finish,” he says.
Kivu Bioscience, which in 2024 raised $92 million to develop ADCs with fewer off-target effects, has another reason to work with multiple specialist CDMOs to develop its molecules: contingency. “I’ve learned in life that you don’t want to put all your eggs in one basket,” CEO Mohit Trikha says. Once a molecule enters clinical trials, the company needs to ensure uninterrupted supply, and having multiple CDMOs provides a safety net, he says.
Advertisement
The multi-CDMO model also allows the company to work with the players that are best at what they do, Trikha adds. The approach requires a high level of coordination with the various drug services firms, “But this is not our first rodeo,” he says. “So, project coordination, project management, and project leadership are very much in our mantra.”
As companies develop new generations of ADCs, several of which are making their way closer to FDA approval, experts such as Dowdy say the market will have a place for all kinds of CDMOs. “Some [CDMOs] will become more global players, and some might be more regional players,” he says.
Aayushi Pratap
is a pharma business reporter at C&EN.
