Regulatory Agencies.content:
By
Joseph Blake
Published: Aug 11 2026, 10:11 AM EDT
Share on Facebook
Share on Twitter
Share on LinkedIn
Share on Reddit
Share on Flipboard
Share on Pocket
CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - DECEMBER 11: In this photo illustration, food products manufactured by Mondelez and Coca-Cola are shown on December 11, 2024 in Chicago, Illinois. Both companies are among those named in a lawsuit that accuses major food companies of marketing ultra-processed and addictive foods to children.
Illustration by Scott Olson/Getty Images
At least 111 food chemicals currently found in sports drinks, snack bars, and breakfast cereals on American grocery store shelves have never been reviewed by any government body for safety — and they entered the U.S. food supply legally, under a regulatory gap the federal government formally moved to close Monday for the first time in 65 years. The Food and Drug Administration published a
proposed rule in the Federal Register
on August 11, 2026 that would, if finalized, require any company introducing a food ingredient under the "Generally Recognized as Safe" (GRAS) designation to notify the agency in writing before marketing it — ending a practice in which companies have been permitted to quietly certify their own ingredients as safe without telling regulators at all.
This is the first mandatory GRAS notification requirement in the 65-year history of the GRAS regulatory framework. More fundamentally, it inverts the legal presumption that has governed food ingredient oversight since 1958: under the proposed rule, a substance introduced without a filed GRAS notice would be treated by the FDA as presumptively
not
safe — reversing a burden of proof that has sat with the agency, not the manufacturer, for more than six decades. "For decades, the GRAS loophole has allowed companies to secretly introduce novel chemicals into our food without meaningful oversight or transparency," Emily Broad Leib, faculty director of the Harvard Law School Food Law and Policy Clinic,
said in March
. The public comment period runs 120 days from August 11, closing December 9, 2026. Comments may be submitted at Regulations.gov under Docket No. FDA-2025-N-3262.
The timing of the announcement matters: the rule was published as the Environmental Working Group's March 2026 investigation had already documented 111 chemicals currently in store products that had never been reviewed, giving the regulatory action an immediately concrete context.
Read more:
Ultra-Processed Food Labels Steer Diets Wrong, Harvard Study of 200,000 Finds
How Did 111 Chemicals Enter Your Food Without FDA Review?
The GRAS concept traces to the Food Additives Amendment of 1958, which Congress passed to exempt obviously safe, time-tested ingredients — vinegar, salt, baking soda — from full premarket approval. The law's logic was sound: the agency did not need clinical trials to certify that table salt was safe. But the legislation left a critical gap: it did not specify who gets to decide whether something qualifies as GRAS, and it did not require that the FDA be informed when a company makes that determination on its own.
For roughly the first two decades, the system functioned close to its intent. Then, in the 1970s, regulations opened a route for manufacturers to conduct their own expert-panel reviews and reach their own GRAS conclusions without notifying anyone. In 1997, the FDA formalized a voluntary notification program — but companies remained free to bypass it entirely. A July 2025 Environmental Working Group analysis found that nearly 99% of food chemicals introduced since 2000 entered the market through the self-affirmed GRAS pathway rather than through any form of FDA review. In raw terms: since 2000, companies filed formal petitions for FDA approval of new substances only 10 times; they self-affirmed 756 other new chemicals as GRAS without notifying the agency.
A March 2026 EWG follow-up
identified 111 of those self-affirmed chemicals
currently found in products on store shelves that had never been subjected to any public government safety review, with 49 of them appearing in thousands of products listed in the USDA's Branded Foods Database. The list includes plant extracts, alternative proteins, and supplement ingredients — some of which companies also used as a backdoor to bypass the separate New Dietary Ingredient notification requirement that applies to supplements.
"This is a wake-up call for every American who assumes the FDA is reviewing the safety of chemicals in their food," said Melanie Benesh, EWG's vice president for government affairs,
reacting to Monday's proposed rule
. "Instead, food and chemical companies are exploiting a loophole to keep both the government and the public in the dark."
The consequences of this system have been invisible largely by design. But one documented case provides a concrete look at what happens when it fails. In 2022, a company that used tara flour as a food ingredient initiated a voluntary recall after the ingredient was linked to roughly 400 adverse event reports describing gastrointestinal distress, liver damage, and hospitalizations. The company had no documentation showing it had reached a formal GRAS conclusion; the FDA had never reviewed the substance. It was only after hundreds of people were harmed that the agency
confirmed in the Federal Register
.
What the Proposed Rule Actually Does
The 48-page proposed rule, formally tracked as RIN 0910-AJ02 and published in the Federal Register at 91 FR 51834, would amend 21 CFR Parts 170 and 570 to make GRAS notification mandatory for any substance introduced into interstate commerce. The rule covers both directly added food ingredients and substances added indirectly, such as from food packaging. Key provisions:
Mandatory notification going forward.
Any company introducing a new substance under the GRAS provision after the rule's effective date must file a full GRAS notice with the FDA — including safety data and the expert rationale underlying the GRAS conclusion. Critically, this is not a premarket approval requirement: companies can still market a substance while the FDA evaluates the notice. The agency proposes to determine whether to file a submission within 45 days of receipt.
Streamlined path for legacy substances.
For the estimated 2,000-plus self-affirmed GRAS substances already on the market, companies would have one year from the effective date to file a "streamlined submission" identifying the substance and its conditions of use — without having to immediately submit the full underlying safety dossier. This takes approximately 31.5 hours of preparation, versus 180 hours for a full GRAS notice. The FDA can then select which substances warrant deeper review and order companies to submit a full notice or food additive petition.
Presumption of non-GRAS for non-notifiers.
The rule's most structurally significant provision: failure to meet the notification requirement would be treated by the FDA as a factor in prioritizing substances for post-market safety review — and uses of substances that have not met the notification requirement are presumed by the FDA not to be GRAS. This is the burden-of-proof reversal at the heart of the proposed rule's significance.
Expanded FDA oversight of prior letters.
The agency would expressly reserve the ability to revisit prior GRAS "no questions" letters, ask follow-up questions, and rescind letters if new information warrants. Law firm Venable noted Monday that
existing holders of prior letters
should recognize their "no questions" letters may not be as secure as previously assumed.
Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas framed the rule directly: "Shifting to a mandatory notification system closes a decades-old information gap, giving the FDA the comprehensive visibility needed to enhance postmarket safety,"
he told reporters Monday
. HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who first directed the FDA to explore this rulemaking in March 2025, called the dual announcement — paired with the submission of the government's first proposed definition of ultra-processed foods to the Office of Management and Budget — a turning point: "These historic actions bring greater transparency to what's in our food and stronger science to federal nutrition policy,"
Kennedy said in Monday's announcement
.
Is FDA Proposing Premarket Approval? No — and That's the Controversy
Food safety advocates had pushed for something stronger: premarket review and approval for all new food chemicals, not just mandatory disclosure of existing GRAS determinations. The Center for Science in the Public Interest welcomed the proposed rule but urged FDA to "fully close the GRAS loophole by requiring premarket review for all new food chemicals." CSPI President Dr. Peter Lurie also raised the enforcement question directly: "Mandatory without enforcement is not mandatory at all."
From the industry side, the rule was received as less disruptive than feared — in part because the notification requirement does not create a premarket barrier. Amaru Sanchez, counsel at law firm Akin, told AgFunderNews that properly conducted self-GRAS determinations should already meet the same substantive scientific standard as submitted GRAS notices — so for companies that did their work rigorously, mandatory notification is more of an administrative change than a fundamental scientific hurdle. But he noted a real resource constraint: "Without more staffing or funding, this is going to be extremely challenging to implement." The FDA already takes roughly a year to process a GRAS notice under the current voluntary system; a surge of mandatory submissions could lengthen that timeline further, creating commercial difficulties for startups awaiting FDA responses before major retailers will source from them.
For companies that did
not
rigorously document their self-GRAS determinations, the picture is starkler. Dr. George Burdock, president of the Burdock Group consulting firm, which has worked with scores of companies on GRAS determinations, was blunt: "I have seen self-GRAS determinations consisting of a two-paragraph memo, signed by some totally unqualified person. Often the person signing off was the owner of the company, a quality assurance person or some chemistry professor at the local junior college,"
he told AgFunderNews
.
Read more:
Ultra-Processed Food Drives a Third of Heart Deaths, GLP-1 Drugs Fight Inflammation
Does FDA Actually Have Legal Authority to Do This?
This is where the proposed rule enters genuinely uncertain territory. In the preamble to its 2016 GRAS final rule, the FDA itself acknowledged that it "may lack express statutory authority" to require mandatory GRAS notifications. That admission now sits awkwardly in the agency's own regulatory record as it proposes to do exactly what it said it might not be able to do.
The proposed rule cites authority under sections 201, 402, 409, and 701 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act — a statutory framework that industry attorneys argue does not squarely authorize mandatory notification. The Supreme Court's 2024 elimination of Chevron deference in
Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo
means courts will now independently interpret statutory ambiguity rather than deferring to agency readings, making a legal challenge meaningfully harder for the agency to withstand than it would have been even two years ago. Jonathan Emord, general counsel at the Alliance for Natural Health, told AgFunderNews that legal challenges are "likely," and Morrison Foerster partner Brian Sylvester advised clients not to "assume that any mandatory submissions will ultimately be required" — specifically noting that "the legal question remains whether the FDCA actually gives FDA authority to impose a mandatory notification requirement without congressional action,"
according to AgFunderNews reporting
.
Kennedy himself acknowledged the gap. During the August 10 announcement, he called on Congress to "give FDA the additional tools it needs to keep pace with the changing food supply" — a notable signal that the administration may view its own proposed rule as a placeholder pending legislation,
Spectrum News reported
. On the legislative track, Senator Roger Marshall (R-KS) introduced the Better Food Disclosure Act of 2025 (S.3122) in November, co-sponsored by Senators Rick Scott and Katie Britt, which would amend the FD&C Act directly to mandate GRAS notifications with statutory authority. Senator Ed Markey's (D-MA) Ensuring Safe and Toxic-Free Foods Act (S.2341) takes a similar approach from the other side of the aisle. The acting FDA commissioner told reporters that
discussions with Congress on legislative options
have been bipartisan.
A final rule, if the proposed rule survives comment and legal challenge, is estimated to be two to three years away. In the meantime, the 111 chemicals that entered the U.S. food supply without review remain in the products that contain them.
First Federal Definition of Ultra-Processed Foods Also Moves Forward
Monday's dual announcement included a second action that could prove equally consequential over time. HHS and USDA submitted to the Office of Management and Budget what would be the first federal government definition of ultra-processed foods (UPFs). No details about the specific definition were released at announcement time, but the move converts what has been a research category — primarily defined by the NOVA classification system developed by epidemiologist Carlos Monteiro at the University of São Paulo — into a potential regulatory category with downstream implications for school meal programs, SNAP purchasing standards, and federal nutrition guidance.
The government has been working toward this definition since July 2025, when FDA and USDA issued a
joint Request for Information
. The comment period closed in October 2025, drawing mixed responses: supporters argued a standard definition was long overdue for research consistency; critics warned that classification based on processing steps rather than nutritive content could penalize nutritionally sound foods. The definition now moves through OMB review before it can be formally proposed for public comment.
The timing of the definition's advancement alongside the GRAS rule is not coincidental. Both actions are part of the MAHA (Make America Healthy Again) regulatory agenda, and both address the same underlying question: what should count as adequate federal oversight of what Americans eat?
What Can Readers Do Now
The practical near-term impact on grocery store shelves is limited. The proposed rule does not order recalls, ban existing ingredients, or require companies to prove safety of what they are already selling. But the regulatory shift creates real leverage points for consumers and advocates.
Readers can submit public comments through December 9, 2026, at Regulations.gov, Docket No. FDA-2025-N-3262. Comments that document specific ingredients currently in use without FDA review, or that make the case for stronger enforcement mechanisms or premarket review, carry particular weight in rulemaking.
For those interested in which specific products contain the 111 unreviewed chemicals identified by EWG, the USDA's Branded Foods Database (available at fdc.nal.usda.gov) allows ingredient-level searching by name, and the EWG's analysis mapped 49 of the 111 chemicals to thousands of products in that database. The EWG maintains an
ongoing food ingredient guide
at EWG.org.
For the food industry, the clock on documenting self-affirmed GRAS determinations began Monday.
Frequently Asked Questions
What is the GRAS loophole, and why does it matter for what I eat?
GRAS — "Generally Recognized as Safe" — is the legal designation that exempts food ingredients from FDA premarket review and approval if they are already widely recognized by experts as safe. The loophole that the FDA's proposed rule targets is the self-affirmation pathway: under existing rules, a company can conduct its own expert review, conclude that a new substance is GRAS, and begin selling food products containing it without ever notifying the FDA. No federal agency reviews the ingredient, no public record is created, and no government body can confirm the safety conclusion is well-founded. An EWG analysis found that nearly 99% of food chemicals introduced since 2000 entered the market through this pathway, not through formal FDA review. The proposed rule would end self-affirmation without disclosure — but it does not require premarket approval, and it does not retroactively ban or require proof of safety for the thousands of substances already in use.
What are the 111 unreviewed chemicals, and should I avoid them?
The 111 substances identified in EWG's March 2026 analysis include plant extracts, alternative proteins, supplement ingredients used as food additives, and other novel substances introduced since 2000 through the self-affirmation route. EWG itself notes that being on this list does not mean a substance is harmful — it means the company's safety determination was never reviewed by regulators, so no independent confirmation of safety exists in the public record. The lack of review creates uncertainty, not a proven danger. Readers who want to search specific products can use the USDA Branded Foods Database at fdc.nal.usda.gov and cross-reference ingredient names against
EWG's research findings
.
Does the proposed rule actually stop companies from using unreviewed ingredients?
Not immediately, and potentially not at all without Congressional action. The proposed rule is in its comment stage, with a final rule likely two to three years away if it survives legal challenge. Even when finalized, it would require notification — not premarket approval — for new ingredients. Companies can still market a substance while the FDA evaluates their notification. For ingredients already on the market under self-affirmed GRAS status, companies would have one year after the rule takes effect to file a simplified disclosure. Whether FDA has the statutory authority to impose even this requirement is contested; the agency's own prior regulatory record acknowledged it "may lack express statutory authority" to mandate notifications, and the Supreme Court's 2024 elimination of Chevron deference means courts will now interpret that ambiguity independently.
Venable LLP's legal analysis
advises companies to assess their existing dossiers without assuming mandatory submissions will ultimately be required.
How do I comment on the FDA's proposed rule?
The 120-day public comment period opened August 11, 2026, and closes December 9, 2026. Submit comments electronically at Regulations.gov by searching for Docket No. FDA-2025-N-3262, titled "Substances Generally Recognized as Safe." Paper comments may be sent to Dockets Management Staff, FDA, 5630 Fishers Lane, Rm. 1061, Rockville, MD 20852. Comments are publicly visible once reviewed. Comments focused on specific ingredients or enforcement mechanisms will likely carry more analytical weight than general statements. Readers can also contact their Congressional representatives to support legislation that would provide express statutory authority for mandatory GRAS notification — the Better Food Disclosure Act (S.3122) and the Ensuring Safe and Toxic-Free Foods Act (S.2341) are the primary pending bills.

Regulatory Agencies.content:
Reviewed by Dietitian Madeline Peck, RDN, CDN
Key Points
Peptides are short chains of amino acids that can be made synthetically for medical purposes.
An FDA committee just voted to ease regulations on six popular peptides.
There are still many unanswered questions about their safety and long-term effects.
If you’re unfamiliar with the latest peptide craze, a quick Google search will do the trick. You’ll find fitness influencers, celebrities and even Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., touting their purported benefits. And with names like GHK-CU, Thymosin Beta-4 and MOTS-c, it can feel like you’re deciphering a secret code when scanning through the names of some of the internet’s most talked-about peptides.
Peptides have been praised for their supposed ability to support everything from wound healing and metabolism to digestion, sleep and healthy aging.
Until recently, many of the peptides making the rounds on social media could only be legally manufactured and sold for research purposes, which meant people who are already using them were often turning to online retailers operating in a “gray market.”
That’s why the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) recently held a meeting to discuss whether several of these popular peptides—seven, to be exact—should be allowed for broader use. And while FDA scientists were against expanding access to the substances, the agency ultimately recommended that six peptides be added to the compounding eligibility list—meaning they may soon become much easier to access through regulated sources.
Here’s what the science says and what you should know about these controversial products before you decide to seek one out for yourself.
What Are Peptides?
If you’re unfamiliar with peptides in general, you’re probably more familiar with some specific varieties than you realize. Some of the most well-known peptide medications include insulin, oxytocin and GLP-1 medications like Ozempic. Essentially, peptides are short chains of amino acids (the building blocks of protein) that occur naturally in the body and can also be made synthetically for medical and research purposes.
The difference between these widely recognized peptide medications and many of the newer peptides trending online is that they’ve undergone rigorous testing in humans and are FDA-approved for specific uses. They also have established manufacturing standards, dosing guidelines and safety data. Many of the peptides gaining traction on social media haven’t gone through that same level of testing, which is one big reason why they remain controversial.
What Does the FDA Decision Mean?
Because research peptides have become so popular in the ever expanding wellness and longevity conversation, the FDA’s Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (a group of outside advisers to the FDA) held a two-day meeting at the end of July to evaluate whether seven of the most popular wellness peptides should be added to the agency’s 503A bulks list. The bulks list compiles ingredients that licensed compounding pharmacies are allowed to use when making customized prescription medications, even if the ingredient isn’t part of an FDA-approved drug.
Simply put, adding a peptide to the bulks list means that licensed
compounding pharmacies
can legally prepare and dispense it to people with a prescription, making it much easier for consumers to access legally than when it was confined to the research market.
It’s important to note that FDA scientists did not support expanding access to the seven peptides. In documents submitted ahead of the two-day meeting, they argued that there is little clinical data demonstrating the peptides’ effectiveness for their promoted uses and that important questions about their long-term safety remain unanswered.
Going against the FDA scientists’ recommendations, the advisory panel voted narrowly to recommend adding six of the seven peptides to the compounding eligibility list. That doesn’t mean the peptides have officially been added to the 503A bulks list just yet. The committee’s vote is advisory, meaning the FDA must still review the recommendation and decide whether to move forward with any regulatory changes.
Advertisement
Which Peptides May Get Approved?
The six peptides that were recommended to be added to the compounding eligibility list—and the uses they’re most commonly promoted or studied for—include:
BPC-157:
Gut health
and connective tissue repair
KPV:
Anti-inflammatory effects
and gut health
TB-500:
Tissue repair and wound healing
MOTS-c:
Glucose metabolism and
muscle health
Semax:
Cognitive function
Epitalon:
Sleep
Emideltide, which has been investigated for insomnia and pain relief, was the seventh peptide discussed during the meeting. However, it was the only one that was not recommended to be added to the compounding eligibility list.
What Are the Risks?
If you’re wondering why this decision has been so controversial, here’s one reason: In 2023, the FDA placed these six peptides—along with 13 others—on a list of substances it considered too risky for compounding pharmacies to use. Then, somewhat unexpectedly, the agency removed the seven peptides discussed at this recent meeting from the high-risk list in April, paving the way for the advisory committee to potentially loosen regulations.
FDA scientists say there’s still little to no clinical trial data supporting the safety or effectiveness of these peptides for their promoted uses, as most of the research done thus far has been animal research. They also note that peptides carry a relatively high risk of triggering
immune reactions
, including serious allergic responses like anaphylaxis, because the body may recognize them as foreign substances.
There are plenty of other unanswered questions, too. Researchers still don’t know whether these peptides are safe for people with certain health conditions, whether they interact with common medications or whether their safety and effectiveness differ depending on how they’re taken, such as by injection, oral capsule or nasal spray.
Additionally, because these peptides haven’t gone through the same rigorous testing as well-known peptide medications like insulin or
GLP-1 drugs
, there are still significant gaps in what we know about their safety and effectiveness. Manufacturing quality can also vary depending on where the peptides come from, increasing the risk of impurities or inconsistencies in the final product.
Are There Any Benefits?
While scientists have raised concerns about expanding access to these peptides, there is a potential benefit. Until now, people seeking these products have relied on online retailers operating through a “gray market,” where product quality and purity can be difficult to verify.
If the FDA ultimately accepts the advisory committee’s recommendation, people obtaining these peptides through licensed pharmacies can rest assured that the products were prepared under sterile environments and contain the specific peptide they claim to contain. That could reduce some of the risks associated with purchasing peptides from unregulated online sources. Still, it doesn’t change the fact that there are still significant questions about their safety and effectiveness.
Our Expert Take
The advisory committee’s vote on these six peptides is not binding—it’s a recommendation. Before any of these peptides can officially be added to the 503A bulks list, the FDA must review the committee’s advice and decide whether to accept, modify or reject it.
For now, we’re choosing to follow the recommendations of FDA scientists and proceed with caution. While these six peptides may become more accessible in the future, there are still major unanswered questions about their safety, effectiveness and long-term effects. At this point, there is no clear timeline for when the FDA will announce its final decision on whether these peptides will be added to the 503A bulks list. Until then, it’s important to keep in mind that increased access does not necessarily mean a product has been proven to be safe or effective.

Regulatory Agencies.content:
VueJect
®
strengthens Bracco's integrated CEUS ecosystem by enabling more standardized, efficient contrast administration in cardiology imaging
MILAN
,
Aug. 11, 2026
/PRNewswire/ -- Bracco Imaging today announced that VueJect
®
, its first dedicated ultrasound contrast delivery system engineered to support cardiology imaging specifically, has received 510(k) clearance from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and authorization from Health Canada. These regulatory milestones represent the first step in Bracco's broader global commercialization strategy for VueJect, reinforcing the company's long-term commitment to advancing contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS). VueJect will initially be available in the United States and Canada, with additional regulatory submissions planned in other markets.
Bracco Logo
VueJect expands Bracco's growing CEUS ecosystem by providing a dedicated contrast delivery solution designed to:
Improve workflow efficiency
through a streamlined contrast administration process
Reduce operator variability
leading to consistency during contrast administration
Enable continuous
administration
of ultrasound contrast agents to support more consistent enhancement during cardiac imaging procedures.
"
VueJect represents a significant strategic milestone for Bracco as we continue investing in innovations that advance contrast-enhanced ultrasound worldwide
," said
Fulvio Renoldi Bracco
, Vice Chairman and CEO, Bracco Imaging. "
Beginning with regulatory approvals in the United States and Canada, VueJect further advances our integrated ultrasound portfolio and reflects our commitment to expanding access to innovative diagnostic solutions around the world
."
"
VueJect
is a defining addition to our CEUS ecosystem, adding a dedicated injector to our Ultrasound-Enhancing Agent portfolio that is able to administer Lumason/SonoVue in dilution in Echocardiography procedures,
" said
Luca Frazzoli
, Global Head of Ultrasound, Bracco Imaging. "
As we bring this technology to more markets, we expect it to change what sonographers and physicians come to expect from contrast administration, setting a new standard for consistency and confidence in everyday practice
."
"
FDA clearance and Health Canada authorization mark an important milestone for clinicians across North America
," said
Robert Mitchell
, MBA, Director, Ultrasound Platform, Americas. "
VueJect
provides cardiac sonographers with a more standardized approach to contrast administration, helping deliver more consistent CEUS examinations, day in and day out
."
Following these regulatory milestones in the United States and Canada, Bracco is preparing for commercial launch while advancing plans for future regulatory submissions in additional global markets. VueJect marks the latest step in Bracco's investment in contrast-enhanced ultrasound.
VueJect has received 510(k) clearance from the U.S. FDA and is licensed by Health Canada under Medical Device License No. 115637. For complete operating instructions, warnings, precautions, and other important safety information, refer to the instructions for use.
About Bracco
Bracco Group, founded in 1927, is a global leader in diagnostic imaging, committed to advancing healthcare and improving people's lives by shaping the future of prevention and precision medicine.
The company operates in the healthcare sector across more than 100 countries with a workforce of over 4,000 employees and consolidated annual revenues of approximately €2 billion, 88% generated by international markets.
With a strong commitment to innovation - investing around 9% of its reference turnover in Research & Development - Bracco develops and provides a broad portfolio of pharmaceutical products for diagnostic imaging, including contrast agents for X-ray, Computed Tomography (CT), and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), as well as microbubbles for Contrast Enhanced Ultrasound (CEUS), and Molecular Imaging through radioactive tracers and novel PET imaging agents, alongside AI-based solutions. It is also a global market leader in advanced contrast management technologies for cardiovascular angiography and radiology imaging.
Discover more at
www.bracco.com
.
VUEJECT is a registered trademark of Bracco Imaging S.p.A.

BEIJING, Aug. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Datasea Intelligent Technology Ltd. (NASDAQ: DTSS) ("Datasea" or the "Company"), a technology company focused on acoustic high-tech and AI multimodal digital solutions, today announced that Shuhai Jingwei (Shenzhen) Information Technology Co., Ltd. ("Shuhai Jingwei"), the Company's variable interest entity in China, has completed establishment registration and device listing with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration ("FDA") for its NeuroVibe Biofeedback System, including products NV-02 and NV-03. The products are listed under FDA product code HCC as Class II 510(k)-exempt biofeedback medical devices within the Neurology regulatory area. FDA establishment registration and device listing do not constitute FDA approval, clearance or authorization of the establishment or the listed devices.
Innovative Vibro-Acoustic Neuromodulation Technology Provides a New Non-Pharmacological Pathway for Clinical Applications
The Company believes that Shuhai Jingwei's initiation of FDA establishment registration and device listing for NeuroVibe, and the products' listing as Class II 510(k)-exempt biofeedback medical devices, is one step forward from the research and development stage to a more clearly defined, regulated product platform with a potential for commercial deployment. It is a key step in translating technological value into clinical and market applications.
The initiation of NeuroVibe's device listing is an important step in Datasea's international commercialization strategy," said Zhixin Liu, Chief Executive Officer of Datasea. "NeuroVibe integrates acoustic intelligence, AI-assisted analysis and non-invasive brain-computer interface technology. We believe this milestone strengthens Datasea's positioning in next-generation brain health technology and it lays the foundation for product iteration, market validation and U.S. and global adoption."
Technology Architecture: A Non-Invasive Platform Combining Acoustic AI and Closed-Loop Biofeedback
NeuroVibe is designed as a non-invasive biofeedback platform integrating four core technology modules: (1) acoustic stimulation, which uses acoustic input at specific frequencies to modulate neural states; (2) tricuspid valve annulus size (tVAS) neuromodulation, or transcranial vibro-acoustic stimulation, which enables non-invasive neuromodulation; (3) electroencephalogram (EEG) signal acquisition, which collects and analyzes brainwave physiological signals in real time; and (4) AI-assisted health management, which provides intelligent analysis and feedback optimization based on individual patient data.
Through this architecture, the system is able to collect and analyze human physiological signals and provide real-time biofeedback to support neurological function assessment and training, brain health management and related wellness-oriented applications.
Differentiated Pathway: From Hardware Device to a Data- and Software-Enabled Brain Health Technology Platform
Datasea's differentiated strength lies in its acoustic AI technology pathway. NeuroVibe is not designed merely as an EEG data acquisition device. Rather, it is intended to integrate acoustic physical input, neural signal acquisition, AI-driven analysis and feedback mechanisms into a closed-loop system. The Company believes this structure may support the evolution of the product from a single hardware device toward a data- and software-enabled brain health technology platform.
The Company has previously announced two acoustic-driven brain-computer interface (BCI) systems that support its strategic plan to develop innovative medical technology. The first is an acoustic-coupled EEG signal enhancement system, which is designed to enhance EEG signal quality through acoustic physical fields. The second is a closed-loop vibration-enhanced BCI system, which is designed to enable a real-time closed loop between vibration stimulation and neural feedback. These systems are intended to support signal enhancement, individualized feature extraction, feedback regulation and potential integration with intelligent health devices and rehabilitation-support scenarios.
Commercialization Pathway: Focusing on Regulatory-Compliant Application Scenarios and Expanding Non-Pharmacological Intervention Pathways
Datasea expects that NeuroVibe's early commercialization efforts in the U.S. market will focus on regulatory-compliant application scenarios aligned with the product classification and intended use listed. Potential application areas include brain health management, supporting neurological function assessment and dynamic tracking; biofeedback training, enabling real-time visualization of physiological signals and self-regulation; stress relaxation, through vibro-acoustic coupling to modulate the autonomic nervous system; sleep improvement, through closed-loop intervention based on brainwave rhythms; and, cognitive maintenance, including support for attention, memory and other cognitive functions.
The Company believes that with the growing demand for non-pharmacological and non-invasive health technologies, NeuroVibe's technology pathway represents immense potential for the expansion of its medtech product applications.
Company Outlook
Datasea believes that Shuhai Jingwei's initiation of NeuroVibe's listing as Class II 510(k)-exempt biofeedback medical devices further strengthens the Company's strategic positioning in acoustic intelligence, AI-driven health technology and non-invasive neurotechnology. The Company plans to continue advancing product iteration, regulatory compliance, channel development and application validation with the goal of building a scalable acoustic AI technology platform for brain health, intelligent interaction and the global health technology market.
About Datasea Intelligent Technology Ltd. (NASDAQ: DTSS)
Datasea Intelligent Technology Ltd. is a Nasdaq-listed technology holding company focused on acoustic high-tech innovation and AI-powered multimodal digital solutions. The Company focuses on the development and commercialization of products, services, and solutions across acoustic high-tech and AI agent multimodal digitalization.

Regulatory Agencies.content:
VRTX
AMLX
PRAX
The pharmaceutical sector differs from many industries as stock performance often depends less on near-term results and more on the success of products in development. For biotech companies, clinical and regulatory developments can sharply alter valuations by changing expectations for a drug's safety, efficacy and commercial potential.
Pipeline milestones are therefore key stock catalysts. Clinical data can validate or undermine a candidate, while regulatory decisions can bring it closer to commercialization. Late-stage data and regulatory milestones generally have a significant impact on stock prices as they offer more clarity on a drug's approval prospects.
Against this backdrop,
Vertex Pharmaceuticals
VRTX,
Amylyx Pharmaceuticals
AMLX,
Praxis Precision Medicines
PRAX and
BridgeBio Pharma
BBIO stand out for having notable pipeline/regulatory developments during the second half of 2026. With multiple clinical and regulatory milestones spanning pain, metabolic disorders, neurological diseases and rare genetic conditions, these companies offer several potentially meaningful catalysts, making the four biotech stocks particularly compelling investment opportunities.
Vertex Pharmaceuticals
The key near-term catalyst for Vertex is the FDA’s pending decision on a biologics license application for accelerated approval of povetacicept in adults with IgA nephropathy (IgAN), scheduled for Nov. 30, 2026. Acquired from Alpine Immune Sciences, povetacicept is being developed as a potential best-in-class therapy for multiple B-cell-mediated diseases and could help Vertex expand beyond its established cystic fibrosis franchise.
Year to date, VRTX shares have gained 15.6% compared with the industry’s 5.2% growth.
The upcoming FDA decision could be particularly important given povetacicept’s potential role in establishing Vertex’s presence in nephrology. If approved, povetacicept would become Vertex’s first commercialized therapy in nephrology, creating a potential new source of product revenues and growth. The company is also advancing povetacicept in primary membranous nephropathy, another B-cell-mediated disease, and has completed the phase IIB portion of the mid- to late-stage program. Conversely, a regulatory setback could delay the candidate’s commercial prospects and weaken expectations for its contribution to Vertex’s longer-term growth. VRTX currently carries a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold). You can see
the complete list of today’s Zacks #1 (Strong Buy) Rank stocks here
.
Amylyx Pharmaceuticals
Amylyx's lead candidate, avexitide, a GLP-1 receptor antagonist, is being developed for post-bariatric hypoglycemia, a condition for which there are currently no FDA-approved therapies. The key near-term catalyst is top-line results from the phase III LUCIDITY study, which Amylyx expects to report in the third quarter of 2026. The study has completed enrollment, with its primary endpoint being the reduction in the composite of Level 2 and Level 3 hypoglycemic events through Week 16.
Year to date, AMLX shares have soared 87.6% against the industry’s 1.5% decline.
The upcoming readout could be particularly important given avexitide’s central role in Amylyx’s pipeline. Earlier clinical studies have demonstrated consistent, dose-dependent effects, providing a supportive backdrop ahead of the pivotal readout. If the phase III study is successful and avexitide is subsequently approved, Amylyx aims to launch the drug commercially in 2027. This would give the company its first marketed drug and a potential recurring source of product revenues, making the LUCIDITY outcome a significant inflection point. Conversely, an unfavorable result could materially weaken avexitide’s regulatory and commercial prospects. Amylyx is also exploring avexitide in congenital hyperinsulinism. AMLX currently carries a Zacks Rank #3.
Praxis Precision Medicines
A potential FDA approval for relutrigine in genetically defined developmental epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs) is Praxis' most prominent second-half catalyst. The new drug application (NDA) is supported by positive results from the registrational cohort of the phase II/III EMBOLD study, which met its primary efficacy objective, demonstrating a 53% placebo-adjusted reduction in monthly motor seizures over 16 weeks in patients with SCN2A- and SCN8A-related DEEs. Although the drug initially received priority review with a Sept. 27, 2026, decision date, the FDA extended the review period by three months, establishing a new Dec. 27, 2026, target action date. The mid-cycle meeting was completed without major safety or efficacy concerns identified to date, and no advisory committee meeting is planned.
Year to date, PRAX shares have rallied 24.6% compared with the industry’s 5.3% growth.
The catalyst is not limited to the regulatory decision. The EMERALD study, evaluating relutrigine in patients with broader DEEs, has completed recruitment and is expected to report top-line results in the fourth quarter of 2026. If positive, the study could support a supplemental NDA in 2027, potentially expanding the commercial opportunity beyond the genetically defined SCN2A- and SCN8A-DEE populations covered by the initial application. PRAX currently carries a Zacks Rank #3.
BridgeBio Pharma
FDA action on BBP-418 for limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2I/R9 (LGMD2I/R9) represents BridgeBio's major second-half catalyst. BBP-418 is an investigational oral glycosylation substrate therapy with a unique mechanism of action that could improve muscle, ambulatory and cardiopulmonary function. Its differentiated proposition is particularly notable because, if approved, BBP-418 could become the first and only approved therapy for LGMD2I/R9 and potentially the first approved therapy for any form of limb-girdle muscular dystrophy.
Year to date, BridgeBioshares have gained 10.7% compared with the industry’s 6.8% growth.
The candidate has already cleared a major clinical hurdle. In the phase III FORTIFY study, BBP-418 met all primary and secondary endpoints at the prespecified 12-month interim analysis, with treated participants improving while placebo recipients declined across key measures. The FDA subsequently accepted BridgeBio's NDA for Priority Review and assigned a decision date of Nov. 27, 2026. The agency is not currently planning an advisory committee meeting, further focusing attention on the regulatory decision itself. BridgeBio also intends to initiate studies in younger LGMD2I/R9 patients and in additional LGMD subtypes, providing potential avenues for label expansion if the initial regulatory outcome is favorable. BBIO currently carries a Zacks Rank #3.

What are the defining numbers behind Blister and Thermoform Contract Packaging Services Market growth?
An absolute opportunity of USD 15.4 billion is expected between 2026 and 2036.
Demand Drivers in the Market
Pharmaceutical launch activity creates recurring demand for qualified packaging capacity. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved 46 novel drugs in 2025, while many established medicines also require new strengths, indications or country packs. Contract packagers absorb this variable workload without forcing each product owner to maintain dedicated blister and thermoform lines for every launch profile.
Traceability requirements increase the amount of packaging work attached to each commercial pack. The FDA Drug Supply Chain Security Act framework requires interoperable electronic tracing of certain prescription drugs at package level. Packaging partners therefore need to connect blistering and cartoning with coding, serialization and controlled release of packaging records.
Primary-pack performance remains a technical purchase criterion. FDA guidance describes blister packages as a combination of forming film and lidding material, with the container-closure system expected to protect the dosage form through its shelf life. Moisture-sensitive products can require cold-form structures or barrier laminates, which increases the value of contractors with qualified tooling and material experience.
Material transition is creating additional qualification work. Regulation (EU) 2025/40 on packaging and packaging waste generally applies from August 2026, increasing pressure on packaging design, recyclability and producer responsibility. Pharmaceutical buyers need contractors that can assess alternative structures without disrupting barrier performance, line efficiency or approved specifications.
Outsourcing also converts fixed packaging investment into qualified external capacity. This matters when commercial demand is uncertain, pack versions vary by country or launches require short campaigns. The purchase case improves when a contractor can manage forming, inspection, cartoning and serialization within one validated workflow.
Key Segments Analyzed
Blister Packaging Services account for 47.0% of the Service Category segment in 2026 because primary-pack qualification combines forming, product loading, lidding and seal control within one regulated process.
Pharmaceutical Packaging holds 45.0% of the Application segment in 2026 as solid oral medicines generate recurring demand for unit-dose protection, coding and country-specific commercial packs.
Pharmaceutical Companies represent 49.0% of the End User segment in 2026 because product owners remain responsible for packaging specifications, stability protection and commercial release even when execution is outsourced.
Cold Form Blister Packaging accounts for 43.0% of the Packaging Type segment in 2026 because aluminum-based cold-form structures provide barrier protection for moisture- and light-sensitive formulations.
Polyvinyl Chloride holds 42.0% of the Material Type segment in 2026 because PVC remains widely used as a thermoform blister forming film and works across established pharmaceutical packaging equipment and laminate structures.
Analyst Opinion at Fact.MR
Shambhu Nath Jha, Principal Consultant at Fact.MR, states, “Blister and thermoform outsourcing is increasingly tied to launch flexibility and packaging compliance rather than line capacity alone. Pharmaceutical buyers need contractors that can validate materials, control artwork and serialization, and maintain pack performance through product transfers. Providers that reduce qualification friction while supporting smaller country-specific campaigns can strengthen long-term client relationships.”
Strategic Implications
Contract packagers should align capacity planning with launch variability and smaller country-specific campaigns rather than relying only on long production runs.
Serialization, vision inspection and artwork governance should be integrated into commercial packaging workflows so product owners can reduce handoffs between vendors.
Material-transition programs need barrier testing and line trials before customers can move from PVC or multilayer structures to alternative formats.
Supplier-transfer proposals should quantify tooling, validation and stability requirements because a lower unit price can be outweighed by requalification cost and launch delay.
How does the Blister and Thermoform Contract Packaging Services Market break down by segment?
The market is segmented by Service Category, Application, End User, Packaging Type and Material Type.
Why do Blister Packaging Services lead Service Category?
Blister Packaging Services are projected to account for a 47.0% share in 2026.

Blistering is the point at which a contractor forms the cavity, loads the dose and seals the lidding material around the product. This process directly affects
package integrity
and shelf-life protection, so buyers place more weight on validated tooling and seal control than they do for packaging steps that can be transferred after the primary pack is released.
The service also supports several commercial requirements in one operation. PCI Pharma Services lists
blister packaging
among its primary packaging capabilities, while Almac operates multi-product and humidity-sensitive blistering. These workflows make blistering a recurring outsourced activity across launches and established products.
Why does Pharmaceutical Packaging lead Application?
Pharmaceutical Packaging is projected to account for a 45.0% share in 2026.

Pharmaceutical programs combine barrier protection with regulated identity and release controls. Tablets and capsules can be packed as individual units, while moisture-sensitive products may require higher-barrier structures. Country launches add coding and artwork requirements after the forming process.
The commercial requirement is recurring because approved products remain in supply after launch. Almac reported that its Audubon facility received approval for a multi-product blister pack following a pre-approval inspection, illustrating the validation work attached to commercial blister operations.
Why do Pharmaceutical Companies lead End User?
Pharmaceutical Companies are projected to account for a 49.0% share in 2026.

Pharmaceutical companies lead because they remain accountable for the packaging system even when physical execution is outsourced. They define the forming material, lidding structure, artwork and coding requirements while linking packaging changes to stability and regulatory files.
Outsourcing becomes attractive when a sponsor needs flexible campaign sizes or several regional pack versions. A qualified partner can provide dedicated blister capacity, cartoning and serialization without requiring the product owner to build separate packaging assets for every portfolio need.
Why does Cold Form Blister Packaging lead Packaging Type?

Cold-form
blister packs
are selected when barrier requirements are more demanding than a standard thermoformed cavity can meet. Aluminum-based structures protect sensitive products from moisture, oxygen and light, making tooling and seal integrity central to qualification.
The format carries trade-offs in cavity size and forming speed, so buyers value contractors that can balance product protection with line efficiency. Traditional & Complementary Medicine.content:
Industry & Competitive Context
India's oral care and skin care personal-care categories through the second half of the twentieth century were dominated by multinational players offering products positioned on functional, modern attributes such as foam, whitening, freshness, and fragrance. Vicco Turmeric entered a market dominated by conventional "snow" creams and was not immediately familiar to consumers, who were apprehensive that the turmeric cream might leave a yellow stain on their skin. In oral care, similarly, the market included branded toothpowders and toothpastes from established companies, against which Vicco positioned an Ayurvedic, herb-based alternative.
Vicco distinguished itself early by choosing not to compete on the same functional attributes as multinational entrants. Company materials describe Vicco Vajradanti as the world's first Ayurvedic toothpaste, formulated with 20 rare medicinal natural herbs, at a time when Indian companies were largely adopting foreign technology and formulations. This "swadeshi" (indigenous) framing was reinforced by the historical context of its founding: Vicco was launched in 1952, the year newly independent India held its first general elections, and the brand has been described as an expression of nationalist sentiment through an indigenously developed toothpowder made from Ayurvedic ingredients.
By the time competing Ayurvedic and herbal players such as Patanjali and established FMCG houses such as Dabur and Himalaya expanded aggressively into personal care in the 2000s and 2010s, Vicco was already positioned as a long-established, trusted incumbent in the Ayurvedic category. Notably, Vicco has not competed primarily on price. Reporting has noted that a 100-gram pack of Vicco Vajradanti toothpaste has been priced higher than comparable packs from Colgate, Patanjali, and Pepsodent, indicating that the brand's Ayurvedic-heritage positioning has supported a premium, rather than a value, price point within the category.
Brand Situation Prior to the Modernisation Campaigns (Pre-2019)
For decades, Vicco's marketing relied almost entirely on a single advertising asset. The jingle "Vicco Turmeric, Nahi Cosmetic" is considered among the most recognised jingles in Indian advertising history, reaching mass audiences via national television. The company adapted this jingle into local dialects and distributed it on video tapes, and also advertised heavily during cinema-hall interval breaks.
This reliance on a legacy jingle, rather than celebrity faces, was itself a distinctive strategic choice. Industry commentary has noted that while good advertisements build traction, celebrity endorsements typically help a brand reach younger audiences a lever Vicco largely did not use in its formative decades.
By the late 2010s, however, the brand recognised a generational gap in its customer base. Ahead of its 2019–20 campaign, Vicco ran a print campaign titled "Trusted Ayurveda" showcasing its full brand portfolio and redesigned Vajradanti's packaging. Brand leadership acknowledged the disconnect directly: Shrirang Tembherkar, brand and media manager at Vicco Labs, stated that while the company had a loyal customer base, it recognised a disconnect with millennial consumers, which the brand sought to address.
Strategic Objective
Vicco's stated objective heading into its 2019 relaunch was to preserve brand trust and legacy equity while making the brand relevant to a younger consumer cohort, without abandoning its core Ayurvedic positioning. Sanjeev Pendharkar, Director of Vicco, framed the task explicitly: Vicco Vajradanti had been a household name since 1952 with a large base of loyal users, and the marketing task was to appeal to millennials and make a "pure Ayurvedic paste" part of their daily regimen.
The agency mandate reinforced this dual objective of continuity and renewal. Triton Communications' Creative Head Jyotsna Parikh described the brief as centred on the idea that the jingle was the brand's biggest asset, and that the task was to "remix" it to make it young and modern rather than replace it.
Campaign Architecture & Execution
The regulatory dispute as a marketing asset (1978 onward)
A defining, and unusual, feature of Vicco's brand-building was the way a tax dispute with the Indian government became embedded directly into its core advertising. In 1978, the Central Excise department classified Vicco Vajradanti and Vicco Turmeric Cream as cosmetics rather than herbal/Ayurvedic remedies, which would have subjected the products to cosmetics taxation. Vicco contested this classification in court. The matter proceeded through multiple stages of litigation over subsequent decades, and the Supreme Court ultimately pronounced its final decision in 2007, ruling that Vicco's products, including Vicco Turmeric Cream, should be classified as Ayurvedic medicines and not cosmetics, and were therefore not liable for cosmetics tax.
Rather than treating this as a purely legal matter, Vicco converted the dispute's core claim into its advertising message. The jingle's central line, "Vicco Turmeric nahi cosmetic, Vicco Turmeric Ayurvedic cream," was created during the period of this dispute to reinforce the company's position that its products were Ayurvedic medicines rather than cosmetics, and functioned, in effect, as a public rebuttal directed at the tax authorities.
The 2019–2020 relaunch with Alia Bhatt
In January 2020 (with the ambassador appointment announced in January 2019 according to Vicco's own account, and campaign execution detailed in trade press through early 2020), Vicco engaged actor Alia Bhatt as brand ambassador for Vicco Vajradanti. The campaign, designed and executed by Triton Communications, centred on two core television commercials one musical, retaining the jingle, and one built around a dentist theme to communicate oral-hygiene messaging supported by a series of shorter fifteen-second films based on product variants.
The retained jingle was explicitly treated as the brand's core equity to be carried forward rather than discarded. The new ad film retained the original Vajradanti jingle while reducing the Ayurveda-heavy, problem-solution narrative style of earlier ads, and incorporated a popular star face and dance choreography aimed at building digital presence across platforms such as TikTok. A stated shift in the media strategy was the explicit insertion of digital formats into the media plan, with Bhatt featured across multiple short-format videos and digital content, even as television remained the leading medium.
The rationale for choosing Bhatt was articulated by both parties. Sanjeev Pendharkar stated that the objective was to appeal to millennials and encourage adoption of a "pure Ayurvedic paste" into their daily regimen, and that Alia Bhatt was seen as the right fit for this task. Alia Bhatt, in turn, stated that she had grown up watching Vicco's advertisements in theatres and that they were imprinted in her mind, and described the brand overhaul as a "huge responsibility" given the brand's legacy and market entrenchment.
Influencer and digital extension (2019–2020)
Alongside the celebrity-led relaunch, Vicco extended its turmeric cream brand into influencer-led digital content. The brand ran a "#NoFilter" challenge in association with Big FM, engaging online influencers and Bollywood personalities such as Soha Ali Khan to promote natural, makeup-free beauty in line with the turmeric cream's positioning.
The 2022 relaunch with Sourav Ganguly
In March 2022, Vicco extended its celebrity-association strategy to a second, distinct ambassador for its broader portfolio. Vicco appointed former Indian cricket captain and then-BCCI president Sourav Ganguly as brand ambassador, with campaigns planned across television, print, and digital media. As with the Alia Bhatt campaign, the explicit strategic intent was nostalgia-led recall activation rather than pure reach-building. The company stated the aim was to rekindle nostalgia among audiences who had grown up watching Ganguly's cricketing performances alongside Vicco's television commercials on the same screen. Shrirang Tembhekar, Head of Marketing at Vicco Laboratories, stated that Ganguly's persona naturally aligned with the brand's philosophy of being "strong and trusted," and that this would help leverage the brand across the categories it was targeting. Ganguly himself echoed the nostalgia framing publicly. He described the association as "a fan moment," noting that he often found himself singing Vicco's jingles.
Positioning & Consumer Insight
Vicco's positioning has consistently rested on a single differentiating claim: that its products are Ayurvedic medicinal formulations rooted in indigenous knowledge, not conventional chemical-based cosmetics or FMCG products. This is evident in the product development history itself Vicco Vajradanti was formulated using 18 Ayurvedic ingredients as an indigenous alternative to imported allopathic oral-care options in the immediate post-independence era and in how the brand addressed early consumer skepticism about the turmeric cream. Because the turmeric cream's natural yellow colour and sandalwood fragrance were unfamiliar to a market used to conventional creams, Vicco used direct-demonstration selling, sending salespeople to retailers with mirrors to apply the cream on the spot and dispel concerns about staining.
The consumer insight underlying the celebrity-led relaunches was that legacy recall (the jingle, the brand's decades-long presence) remained a strong latent asset among both older and younger consumers, but needed a contemporary face to convert nostalgia into active purchase consideration among a demographic that had not directly experienced the brand's original 1970s–1990s television campaigns. This is reflected in the deliberate choice to retain, rather than replace, the jingle in the 2019–20 campaign relaunch.
Media & Channel Strategy
Vicco's channel strategy has evolved in three broad, publicly documented phases:
Mass broadcast and cinema-hall era
: Heavy use of national television and cinema-hall interval advertising, with the jingle adapted into regional dialects.
Print and packaging refresh (2019)
: A "Trusted Ayurveda" print campaign across the brand portfolio, alongside a mid-2019 packaging redesign for Vajradanti.
Digital and celebrity-led multi-channel push (2019–2022)
: Insertion of digital formats into the media mix, with short-format video content distributed alongside television as the lead medium; continued use of television, print, and digital media for the 2022 Ganguly campaign. Separately, the brand has used Instagram, Facebook, and YouTube for a mix of promotional, educational, and moment-marketing content aimed at younger audiences.
Business & Brand Outcomes
Vicco has not published campaign-specific sales or market-share results tied to the Alia Bhatt or Sourav Ganguly campaigns in any verified public source reviewed for this case. The following outcomes are documented at the company/group level, not attributable to any single campaign:
Vicco Group's revenue was reported at approximately ₹500 crore as of 2020, consistent with figures reported elsewhere for later years.
Under Gajanan Pendharkar's leadership from 1971, the company's turnover grew from approximately ₹1 lakh to ₹350 crore by 2015; group turnover was reported at approximately ₹500 crore in subsequent reporting.
The company operates factories in Thane, Nagpur, and Goa, has more than 40 products in its portfolio, and exports to 45 countries.
Vicco Laboratories has been accorded "Export House" status by the Government of India's Ministry of Commerce on account of its continuous export activity, and the company states it has received national and international awards in advertising, export, quality, and international trade. The company also states it has been recognised by The Economic Times as one of India's iconic brands.
On the regulatory front, the Supreme Court's 2007 ruling in Vicco's favour legally affirmed the company's core marketing claim that its flagship products are Ayurvedic medicinal preparations rather than cosmetics, a judicial outcome the brand has continued to reference implicitly through its retained jingle.
Strategic Implications
Vicco's brand strategy offers several transferable lessons for legacy, heritage-driven brands operating in categories increasingly contested by both multinational and new-age indigenous competitors.
First, regulatory and legal narratives can be converted into durable brand equity.
Vicco's approach to the 1978–2007 excise classification dispute encoding its legal defence directly into a jingle line rather than treating the litigation as a background compliance matter is a distinctive example of turning a defensive institutional battle into an offensive positioning statement that consumers could recall and repeat for decades.
Second, legacy communication assets can be renovated rather than replaced.
Across both the 2019 Alia Bhatt campaign and, implicitly, the 2022 Ganguly campaign, Vicco's agency and leadership consistently treated the original jingle as the primary brand asset to be preserved, modernising its presentation (tempo, choreography, format) rather than discarding it for an entirely new creative platform. This reflects a conscious strategic bet that decades of accumulated mental availability outweighed the risk of appearing dated.
Third, celebrity endorsement was introduced deliberately and later than category norms
, reflecting a considered trade-off between the brand's historically jingle-led, non-celebrity identity and the reach and youth-relevance benefits that a recognisable face could offer. The explicit rationale given by company leadership a "disconnect with millennials" indicates this shift was insight-led rather than reflexive imitation of category practice.
Fourth, heritage alone is an insufficient long-term strategy without periodic reinvestment in relevance.
The gap between Vicco's peak mass-broadcast era and its 2019 relaunch suggests that even highly distinctive legacy assets require active reinvestment to remain salient across generational cohorts, rather than being assumed to sustain recall indefinitely.
Because Vicco is a privately held company that does not publish detailed financial or marketing-performance disclosures, this case is necessarily bounded by what has been stated in company communications and covered in trade and business press. Readers using this case for strategic analysis should treat the absence of quantified campaign outcomes as a limitation of available public data, not as an indication that such outcomes do not exist.
Discussion Questions
Vicco converted a regulatory dispute (the Central Excise Department's cosmetics classification, 1978–2007) into a core piece of brand communication. Under what conditions is it strategically sound for a brand to embed a legal or regulatory defence directly into consumer-facing messaging, and what are the risks of this approach if the underlying case had been decided differently?
Vicco's 2019 relaunch explicitly retained its original jingle rather than replacing it with a new creative platform, even while introducing a new brand ambassador. Evaluate this as a brand-equity management decision. When should a heritage brand preserve a legacy asset versus retire it in favour of newer creative territory?
Compare Vicco's decision to introduce celebrity endorsement only in 2019 (with Alia Bhatt) after nearly seven decades of jingle-led, largely non-celebrity advertising against category norms in Indian FMCG marketing. What strategic trade-offs does a "late entry" into celebrity endorsement present for a brand with strong pre-existing recall?
Vicco used two brand ambassadors within a three-year period (Alia Bhatt, 2019; Sourav Ganguly, 2022) with distinctly different audience appeals and personas. Assess the coherence of this approach from a brand architecture and consistency standpoint, using the publicly stated rationale for each appointment.
Given the absence of publicly disclosed sales, market-share, or brand-tracking data tied to Vicco's celebrity campaigns, what alternative, publicly observable indicators (e.g., export status, awards, continued group revenue growth) can reasonably be used to assess whether a legacy brand's repositioning strategy is succeeding, and what are the limitations of relying on such indicators?
body_summary_lines: Industry & Competitive Context

India's oral care and skin care personal-care categories through the second half of the twentieth century were dominated by multinational players offering products positioned on functional, modern attributes such as foam, whitening, freshness, and fragrance.

Vicco Turmeric entered a market dominated by conventional "snow" creams and was not immediately familiar to consumers, who were apprehensive that the turmeric cream might leave a yellow stain on their skin.
In oral care, similarly, the market included branded toothpowders and toothpastes from established companies, against which Vicco positioned an Ayurvedic, herb-based alternative.
Vicco distinguished itself early by choosing not to compete on the same functional attributes as multinational entrants.

By

This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies
here
.
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search.
Set us as preferred
“Cooling herbs,” such as peppermint, chrysanthemum, lemongrass and hibiscus, may help the body feel cooler.
Anima Mundi Apothecary, in Venice, offers jars of loose, organic herbs as well as tinctures and sprays to beat the heat.
The store also hosts meditations, sound baths, tarot readings and massages to help bring mind and body into balance.
Rolling heat waves. Unusually high humidity. A supersized
El Niño
on the horizon, which stands to spike temperatures to unprecedented degrees.
Summer in Los Angeles may not have broken any heat records — yet — but the relentless hot weather may be more than you’re able to endure, at least comfortably. Especially without AC at home. Personally, I’ve launched a full-scale assault on the sweltering weather, including consulting heat researchers for
strategies on staying cool
at home.
Which have worked to varying degrees so far.
So what next? I’d been
hearing a lot
about Ayurvedic herbalism, which has been used in India for thousands of years to help people cope with the heat, among other conditions, naturally and holistically. Herbal remedies — in both Ayurvedic and traditional Chinese medicine — are not a medical treatment for heat stroke and other heat illnesses, but they may bring relief in warm weather, some experts say, particularly when prepared by a clinical herbalist.
Advertisement
“You have to, of course, make sure you have enough fluid first — water is key,” says
Dr. Ka-Kit Hui
, director of
UCLA’s Center for East-West Medicine
. “But many of the cooling herbs, like chrysanthemum and honeysuckle, which are anti-inflammatory, and peppermint, for sure, are used for heat symptoms. Some of the chemicals in the herbs are helpful in maintaining the metabolism so that it’s not superfast and generating more heat in the system.”
Peppermint is one of the most popular cooling herbs.
(Deborah Vankin / Los Angeles Times)
Herbs aren’t a cure-all, Hui cautions. They won’t lower your actual body temperature significantly on their own, or every time. Much depends on what’s raising your body temperature in the first place — if you have a fever due to an infection, for example, see a doctor rather than ingesting peppermint.
“But they’re antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory and are cooling,” he says of some herbs. “And they reduce the
feeling
of heat. They work in a mild manner with the body’s physiological system bringing the system back into balance.”
Lifestyle
This common ‘heat wave mistake’ could harm your health as temperatures soar over 95 degrees this weekend
The CDC warns that electric fans can actually raise your body temperature in extreme heat. Learn the safe temperature limits and expert-backed ways to beat the heat.
July 31, 2026
I was still undecided on the benefits of herbs to keep cool. But — willing to try nearly anything on a recent stifling afternoon — I made a trip to
Anima Mundi Apothecary
, in Venice. The “high vibrational” herb shop offers “plant medicines for body, mind & wellness.” It’s the brainchild of clinical herbalist Adriana Ayales, who grew up in Costa Rica with a background in rainforest herbalism. She also trained with shamanic communities throughout Central and South America. Her
Anima Mundi Herbals
is based in Brooklyn, N.Y., where the company manufactures herbal tinctures, elixirs, teas, herbal supplements and other botanicals. It also has shops in Soho in Manhattan as well as Uvita in Costa Rica. The Venice location opened in 2023.
Inside Anima Mundi Apothecary, which houses more than 100 organic or wild herbs.
(Anima Mundi Apothecary)
The apothecary is part herb shop, with a wall of more than 100 organic or wild crafted herbs, in jars, from small farms in Southeast Asia and Costa Rica as well as Oregon, Washington, Vermont and upstate New York; it’s part co-working space, with an adjacent “tonic bar” serving chilled elixirs, mocktails, “longevity shots,” teas and medicinal lattes; and it’s part event space, with a lushly landscaped courtyard adorned with a firepit, rose quartz crystals and blooming white sage, lavender, lemon verbena and passion flower, among other plantings. The apothecary hosts
meditations
,
sound baths
,
tarot card readings
and
massages
there to help bring the mind and body into balance.
The herbs at the shop support Ayurvedic medicine,
traditional Chinese medicine
, rainforest herbalism and American eclectic herbalism, Ayales says. “All of the traditions, including European, we involve in the blending of formulas,” she says. “Every ecosystem has their own set of plants that can greatly help healing in so many ways. It’s medicine for the people, grassroots herbalism that you see throughout the world.”
Advertisement
I had just one thing in mind when I arrived, however: cooling herbs. The AC in my car was on the fritz and I arrived red faced and sweaty. My iPhone overheated on the way over and stopped working immediately upon arrival. A shop attendant shuttled me into a shady spot by the tonic bar, where the mixologist began mixing me cooling drinks. In the meantime, Aria Krylova, who’s worked at Anima Mundi for several years, put out the store’s top cooling agents for me to try.
The Rose Water spritz is popular when temperatures soar in L.A.
(Deborah Vankin / Los Angeles Times)
First on the list: rose water “beauty myst,” which Krylova says is frequently requested during heat waves. “We call it a beauty mist, but it’s used Ayurvedically to cool down the body,” she says. “It’s just rose flower and distilled water. Rose is very anti-inflammatory. I like to put it in the fridge. And you come back home from a hot day, before you’ve turned on the AC, and it feels like heaven.”
She was not incorrect. I spritzed it over my upper body, moistening my cheeks, neck and chest. I do the same with a
water bottle at home
and it’s just as cooling — instantly — but the rose water’s delicious scent left me feeling especially pampered.
Lifestyle
For Subscribers
24 of the best, cheapest and most surprising L.A. pools to beat the heat
Looking for the best Los Angeles pools? Dive into our curated guide to the county’s top affordable public pools, community swim centers and splash zones for sport and play.
June 30, 2026
Krylova then led me to the wall of herbs, offering two cooling blends that can be made into tea at home.
Anima Mundi’s “main cool down blend,” as she described it, contains lemongrass, hibiscus, peppermint and orange peel. “It’s called the Hibiscus Cooler,” Krylova says, adding that the recipe is simple. Add one tablespoon of herbs to about 8 to 12 ounces of hot water. Wait for five to 15 minutes, depending on how strong you want the tea, while the herbs steep. Strain the liquid and cool it in the refrigerator. “It tastes like a floral garden,” Krylova says.
The second tea is a custom blend that Krylova concocted for her partner, who “runs hot.” It has lemon verbena, lemongrass, rose, hibiscus flower, tulsi and peppermint. (Preparation is the same as the above.)
“Lemon verbena is one of the best anti-inflammatory herbs — a lot of times when people are overheated, they tend to feel inflamed,” Krylova says. “And lemongrass is also extremely cooling for the body. Tulsi is considered to be the queen of herbs in Ayurvedic tradition. It’s extremely mineralizing for the body, replenishing. And peppermint is a top herb for cooling down your body quick.”
Advertisement
Finally, Anima Mundi served me two cooling drinks in the garden. Just the sight of the glasses, dewy with condensation on the outside and filled to the rim with clinking ice, nearly chilled my body.
The Hibiscus Sol-Mate, tart and flavorful, is popular in heat waves and during flu season.
(Deborah Vankin / Los Angeles Times)
The Hibiscus Sol-Mate ($7) was a blend of (slightly caffeinated) yerba mate, hibiscus, rose, peppermint and lemongrass, with a fresh lemon slice and a hint of agave. The Tranquility Tea ($7) was composed of chamomile, lemon balm, oatstraw, marshmallow root, jasmine flowers and butterfly pea flowers with tiny flowers floating on top. Both tasted like refreshing iced teas, but the Hibiscus Sol-Mate, a fruit punch red, was more astringent and tart — though flavorful — and the Tranquility Tea, a deep blueberry color, was sweeter and lightly floral tasting.
The Tranquility Tea, sweet and floral-tasting, lives up to its name; the floating flowers are calming.
(Deborah Vankin / Los Angeles Times)
Did any of these herbal concoctions actually cool my body temperature? Unclear. But they were thoroughly enjoyable to consume. And the experience was both calming and refreshing. I bought large bags of loose peppermint and spearmint to use for tea at home.
Bonus: my car smelled sublime — minty and fresh — the entire way home. It was curiously relaxing. The aromatherapy, alone, may have been worth the trip.
